fields.Notes: A six-hour performance in Naples in 1974. The artist stood passive beside a table of 72 objects, including a rose, a scalpel, and a loaded gun, with a note inviting the audience to use them on her. By the end her clothes had been cut off and someone held the gun to her head.

fields.Clue: A woman sits silent and motionless in a chair at a small table, while visitors take turns sitting opposite and meeting her gaze, day after day for about three months.

fields.Title: Surrealism
fields.Artist: André Breton; Salvador Dalí; René Magritte; Max Ernst
fields.Notes: Launched by a manifesto in 1924; its techniques included automatic drawing, frottage, and the exquisite corpse.
fields.Description: A movement that sought to release the unconscious mind through dream imagery, automatism, and startling juxtapositions.
fields.Captions: Salvador Dalí, The Persistence of Memory, 1931 | René Magritte, The Son of Man, 1964 | Max Ernst, The Elephant Celebes, 1921 | René Magritte, The False Mirror, 1929

fields.Title: Impressionism
fields.Artist: Claude Monet; Pierre-Auguste Renoir; Edgar Degas; Camille Pissarro; Berthe Morisot
fields.Notes: Named derisively after Impression, Sunrise at the painters' first independent exhibition, in 1874.
fields.Description: A French movement of loose, broken brushwork capturing the fleeting effects of light, often painted outdoors.
fields.Captions: Claude Monet, Impression, Sunrise, 1872 | J. M. W. Turner's atmospheric work | Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette, 1876

fields.Title: Post-Impressionism
fields.Artist: Paul Cézanne; Vincent van Gogh; Paul Gauguin; Georges Seurat
fields.Notes: The term comes from Roger Fry's 1910 London exhibition Édouard Manet and the Post-Impressionists.
fields.Description: Late 19th-century painting that kept a bright palette but restored solid structure, form, and symbolic meaning.
fields.Captions: Henri Rousseau, A Centennial of Independence, 1892 | Paul Cézanne, The Card Players, 1890–1892 | Georges Seurat, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, 1884–1886 | Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Portrait of Émile Bernard, 1886

fields.Title: Pop art
fields.Artist: Andy Warhol; Roy Lichtenstein; Richard Hamilton; Claes Oldenburg
fields.Notes: Just What Is It That Makes Today's Homes So Different, So Appealing? (1956) is usually called its first work.
fields.Description: Art that took its imagery from advertising, comic strips, packaging, and celebrity, blurring high and low culture.
fields.Captions: Painting by James Gill | Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Cans, 1962 | The American Supermarket exhibition, Bianchini Gallery, New York, 1964

fields.Title: Mannerism
fields.Notes: The name comes from maniera, “style”; Madonna with the Long Neck is its emblem.
fields.Description: The style that followed the High Renaissance: elongated figures, acid colour, crowded space, and deliberate artifice.
fields.Captions: Parmigianino, Madonna with the Long Neck, 1534–40 | Laocoön and His Sons, ancient sculpture rediscovered in 1506 | Ignudi from Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling | Bastiano da Sangallo's copy of Michelangelo's lost Battle of Cascina

fields.Title: Dada
fields.Artist: Marcel Duchamp; Hans Arp; Tristan Tzara; Hannah Höch
fields.Notes: Born at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916; its tools were chance, readymades, sound poetry, and photomontage.
fields.Description: An anti-art movement that answered the slaughter of the First World War with absurdity, provocation, and nonsense.
fields.Captions: First International Dada Fair, Berlin, 1920 | Dada artists in Paris, 1920 | Francis Picabia, Le Saint des saints, 1915

fields.Title: Fauvism
fields.Artist: Henri Matisse; André Derain; Maurice de Vlaminck
fields.Notes: Named when the critic Louis Vauxcelles called the painters at the 1905 Salon d'Automne fauves, “wild beasts”.
fields.Description: A short-lived French movement of vivid, non-naturalistic colour laid on in bold, unmodulated strokes.
fields.Captions: Henri Matisse, Woman with a Hat, 1905 | André Derain, Charing Cross Bridge, London, 1906 | Henri Matisse, Luxe, Calme et Volupté, 1904

fields.Title: Abstract Expressionism
fields.Artist: Jackson Pollock; Willem de Kooning; Mark Rothko; Barnett Newman
fields.Notes: The first American movement to lead the Western avant-garde, split between gestural action painting and colour field.
fields.Description: A postwar New York movement of vast non-figurative canvases, made by energetic gesture or broad fields of colour, conveying the painter's inner life.
fields.Captions: Helen Frankenthaler, The Bay, 1963 | David Smith, Cubi VI, 1963 | Richard Stankiewicz, welded found-metal sculpture (detail)

fields.Title: Cubism
fields.Artist: Pablo Picasso; Georges Braque; Juan Gris
fields.Notes: It moved from an Analytic phase of fragmented, near-monochrome forms to a Synthetic phase of collage and flat colour; Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) is its precursor.
fields.Description: An early 20th-century movement that broke objects into faceted planes seen from several viewpoints at once.
fields.Captions: Pablo Picasso, Girl with a Mandolin, 1910 | Albert Gleizes, Man on a Balcony, 1912

fields.Title: Futurism
fields.Artist: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti; Umberto Boccioni; Giacomo Balla; Gino Severini
fields.Notes: Launched by a manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro in 1909; Unique Forms of Continuity in Space is its best-known sculpture.
fields.Description: An Italian movement glorifying speed, machines, youth, and violence, rendering motion through repeated forms and force-lines.
fields.Captions: Gino Severini, Dynamic Hieroglyphic of the Bal Tabarin, 1912 | Russolo, Carrà, Marinetti, Boccioni, and Severini in Paris, 1912 | Umberto Boccioni, Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, 1913 | Umberto Boccioni, The City Rises (1910), oil on canvas, Museum of Modern Art, New York City

fields.Title: Expressionism
fields.Artist: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner; Wassily Kandinsky; Egon Schiele; Edvard Munch
fields.Notes: Its German groups were Die Brücke (Dresden, 1905) and Der Blaue Reiter (Munich, 1911).
fields.Description: A movement that distorted colour and form to convey inner feeling rather than outward appearance.
fields.Captions: Poster for the film The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, 1920 | Rudolf Steiner, the second Goetheanum, Dornach, 1924–28

fields.Title: Rococo
fields.Artist: Jean-Antoine Watteau; François Boucher; Jean-Honoré Fragonard
fields.Notes: The name comes from rocaille, shell-work; the fête galante was its signature subject.
fields.Description: The light, playful, and ornate 18th-century style that followed the Baroque, full of pastel colour, curves, and amorous scenes.
fields.Captions: Salon de la Princesse, Hôtel de Soubise, Paris | Jean-Honoré Fragonard, The Swing, 1767 | Chelsea porcelain figure group, England | Interior of Rottenbuch Abbey church, Bavaria

fields.Title: Neoclassicism
fields.Artist: Jacques-Louis David; Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres; Antonio Canova
fields.Notes: Sparked by the excavations of Herculaneum and Pompeii and by Winckelmann's writings; Oath of the Horatii (1784) is its manifesto picture.
fields.Description: A late 18th-century revival of ancient Greek and Roman art: moral subjects, clear outline, and restrained composition.
fields.Captions: Antonio Canova, Psyche Revived by Cupid’s Kiss | Michelangelo Maestri, Cupid driving a chariot of griffins, c. 1800 | The Emperor's bathroom, Château de Rambouillet | Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory, pair of spindle vases, 1814, Louvre

fields.Title: Romanticism
fields.Artist: Eugène Delacroix; Théodore Géricault; Caspar David Friedrich; J. M. W. Turner
fields.Notes: The Raft of the Medusa (1818–19) and Liberty Leading the People (1830) are its landmark French pictures.
fields.Description: A movement that valued emotion, imagination, the sublime, and the exotic over Neoclassical reason and order.
fields.Captions: Caspar David Friedrich, Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, 1818 | Eugène Delacroix, The Death of Sardanapalus, 1827 | Philipp Otto Runge, The Morning, 1808 | William Blake, The Little Girl Found, from Songs of Innocence and of Experience, 1794

fields.Title: Realism
fields.Artist: Gustave Courbet; Jean-François Millet; Honoré Daumier
fields.Notes: A Burial at Ornans (1849–50) gave an ordinary village funeral the scale of history painting.
fields.Description: A mid-19th-century French movement that depicted ordinary people and everyday life truthfully, without idealization.
fields.Captions: Gustave Courbet, The Stone Breakers, 1849 | Gustave Courbet, Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet, 1854 | Jean-François Millet, The Gleaners, 1857 | Honoré Daumier, The Third-Class Carriage, c. 1862–1864

fields.Title: Symbolism
fields.Artist: Gustave Moreau; Odilon Redon; Pierre Puvis de Chavannes
fields.Notes: Jean Moréas published its manifesto in Le Figaro in 1886.
fields.Description: A late 19th-century reaction against Realism that evoked ideas, dreams, and myth through suggestion rather than description.
fields.Captions: Gustave Moreau, Oedipus and the Sphinx, 1864 | Arnold Böcklin, Isle of the Dead, 1880

fields.Title: De Stijl
fields.Artist: Piet Mondrian; Theo van Doesburg; Gerrit Rietveld
fields.Notes: Named after the journal launched in 1917; its theory was Neoplasticism, and the Red and Blue Chair and the Schröder House carried it into design.
fields.Description: A Dutch movement reducing art to horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colours, and black, white, and grey.
fields.Captions: Theo van Doesburg, Counter-Composition V, 1924 | Gerrit Rietveld, Rietveld Schröder House, Utrecht, 1924 | Gerrit Rietveld, Red and Blue Chair, 1919–23

fields.Title: Suprematism
fields.Artist: Kazimir Malevich; El Lissitzky; Lyubov Popova
fields.Notes: Announced in 1915 by Black Square, hung across a corner like an Orthodox icon.
fields.Description: A Russian abstract movement of basic geometric forms -- squares, circles, lines -- expressing pure feeling rather than depicting objects.
fields.Captions: Kazimir Malevich, Suprematist Composition, 1915–16 | Kazimir Malevich, Black Square, 1915

fields.Title: Constructivism
fields.Artist: Vladimir Tatlin; Alexander Rodchenko; El Lissitzky; Lyubov Popova
fields.Notes: Its emblem is the unbuilt Monument to the Third International (1919–20).
fields.Description: A Russian movement that rejected art for art's sake in favour of industrial materials and design serving the new Soviet society.
fields.Captions: Vladimir Tatlin, Monument to the Third International (Tatlin's Tower), 1919 | Print shop of Ogonyok magazine, designed by El Lissitzky

fields.Title: Minimalism
fields.Artist: Donald Judd; Carl Andre; Dan Flavin; Agnes Martin
fields.Notes: Frank Stella's “What you see is what you see” became its motto.
fields.Description: Art of plain geometric forms in industrial materials, arranged in serial units that refer to nothing beyond themselves.
fields.Captions: Donald Judd, Untitled, 1988–91, concrete | Dan Flavin, untitled (to Don Judd, colorist)

fields.Title: Conceptual art
fields.Artist: Sol LeWitt; Joseph Kosuth; Lawrence Weiner; Yoko Ono
fields.Notes: Touchstones include Paragraphs on Conceptual Art (1967), which called the idea “a machine that makes the art”, and One and Three Chairs (1965).
fields.Description: Art in which the idea behind the work matters more than its look or craft, often presented as text, instructions, or documentation.
fields.Captions: Sol LeWitt, a wall drawing in Spoleto | Lawrence Weiner

fields.Title: Hudson River School
fields.Artist: Thomas Cole; Frederic Edwin Church; Albert Bierstadt; Asher Durand
fields.Notes: Its later generation carried the style to the Rockies, Yosemite, and the Andes.
fields.Description: A 19th-century American school of romantic landscape painting that celebrated the wilderness of the Catskills and the West.
fields.Captions: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow, 1836 | Thomas Cole, A View of the Two Lakes and Mountain House, Catskill Mountains, Morning, 1844 | Frederic Edwin Church, Niagara, 1857

fields.Title: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
fields.Artist: Dante Gabriel Rossetti; John Everett Millais; William Holman Hunt
fields.Notes: Founded in London in 1848 by seven young men who signed their works “PRB”; John Ruskin championed them.
fields.Description: A group of English painters who rejected academic convention for the bright colour, sharp detail, and sincerity of art before the High Renaissance.
fields.Captions: William Holman Hunt, The Hireling Shepherd, 1851 | Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Proserpine, 1874, with Jane Morris as model | Ford Madox Brown, The Last of England depicting an emigrating couple, 1855

fields.Title: Orphism
fields.Artist: Robert Delaunay; Sonia Delaunay; František Kupka
fields.Notes: Named in 1912 by the poet Guillaume Apollinaire, after the mythical singer Orpheus.
fields.Description: An offshoot of Cubism in which pure, contrasting colour rather than form carries the picture, often in circular rhythms.
fields.Captions: Robert Delaunay, Circular Forms, Moon No. 1, 1913 | Robert Delaunay, Rhythm, Joy of Life, 1930 | Robert Delaunay, one of his Eiffel Tower paintings, 1910s

fields.Title: Ukiyo-e
fields.Artist: Katsushika Hokusai; Utagawa Hiroshige; Kitagawa Utamaro
fields.Notes: Its flat colour and bold cropping fed Japonisme and reshaped European painting from the 1860s.
fields.Description: Japanese woodblock prints and paintings of the “floating world” of actors, courtesans, travel, and landscape.
fields.Captions: Oniji Ōtani III | Kitagawa Utamaro, Kushi (Comb), c. 1785

fields.Title: Bauhaus
fields.Artist: Walter Gropius; Wassily Kandinsky; Paul Klee; László Moholy-Nagy
fields.Notes: Founded in Weimar in 1919, it moved to Dessau and Berlin and closed under Nazi pressure in 1933; its émigré teachers spread its ideas worldwide.
fields.Description: A German art school that united fine art, craft, and industrial design, aiming at simple, functional objects fit for mass production.
fields.Captions: The workshop wing of the Bauhaus Dessau, designed by Walter Gropius, 1925–26 | Costumes for Oskar Schlemmer's Triadic Ballet, 1922

fields.Title: Chiaroscuro
fields.Notes: Italian for “light-dark”; in printmaking the word also names woodcuts printed from several tone blocks.
fields.Description: Modelling form through strong contrasts of light and dark.
fields.Captions: Giovanni Baglione, Divine Love Conquering Earthly Love, 1602–03 | Hans Holbein the Younger, Christ at Rest, 1519, chiaroscuro drawing | Bartolomeo Coriolano, Virgin and Child, chiaroscuro woodcut, 1630–55

fields.Title: Tenebrism
fields.Artist: Caravaggio; Artemisia Gentileschi; Georges de La Tour
fields.Notes: From the Italian tenebroso, “murky”; Caravaggio's followers, the Caravaggisti, spread it across Europe.
fields.Description: Chiaroscuro pushed to violent extremes: figures lit as if by a single source against deep darkness.
fields.Captions: Caravaggio, John the Baptist in the Wilderness, 1604 | Jusepe de Ribera, Martyrdom of Saint Andrew, 1628

fields.Title: Sfumato
fields.Notes: Italian for “smoked”; the Mona Lisa's face is its most famous demonstration.
fields.Description: Tone graded so softly that outlines vanish, “without lines or borders, in the manner of smoke”.
fields.Captions: Detail of the face of Mona Lisa showing the use of sfumato, particularly in the shading around the eyes | Raphael, Madonna del Prato, 1505–06

fields.Title: Pointillism
fields.Notes: Seurat called his method chromoluminarism; critics coined “pointillism” in the late 1880s to mock it.
fields.Description: Painting in small separate dots of unmixed colour that combine in the viewer's eye.
fields.Captions: Georges Seurat, Parade de cirque, 1887–88 | Vincent van Gogh, Self Portrait, 1887, using pointillist technique | Maximilien Luce, Morning, Interior, 1890 | Georges Seurat, Bathers at Asnières, 1884

fields.Title: Impasto
fields.Artist: Vincent van Gogh; Rembrandt; Frank Auerbach
fields.Notes: From the Italian for “kneaded”; it catches real light, so the paint surface itself becomes part of the image.
fields.Description: Paint laid on so thickly that it stands up from the surface and keeps the marks of the brush or knife.
fields.Captions: Still Life: Vase with Pink Roses (1890) | Cordelia Wilson, Taos Mountain, Trail Home, c. 1920 | Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889

fields.Title: Trompe-l'œil
fields.Notes: French for “deceive the eye”; Pliny tells of Zeuxis painting grapes so real that birds pecked at them.
fields.Description: Illusionistic painting convincing enough to be mistaken for the real object.
fields.Captions: Ceiling of the Treasure Room of the Archaeological Museum of Ferrara, Italy, painted in 1503–1506 | Still life, Pompeii, c. 70 CE | Evert Collier, Trompe l'œil with Writing Materials | Pere Borrell del Caso, Escaping Criticism, 1874

fields.Title: Contrapposto
fields.Notes: Italian for “counterpose”; Greek sculptors developed it in the early 5th century BCE (the Kritios Boy), and the Renaissance revived it.
fields.Description: A standing pose with the weight on one leg, so that the hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions.
fields.Captions: Kritios Boy, c. 480 BCE | Italian bronze figure, 3rd–1st century BCE | Venus de Milo, Louvre

fields.Title: Collage
fields.Artist: Pablo Picasso; Georges Braque; Kurt Schwitters
fields.Notes: The Cubists brought it into fine art in 1912; the name comes from the French coller, “to glue”.
fields.Description: Pasting paper, fabric, and other materials onto a flat surface as part of the picture.
fields.Captions: Kurt Schwitters, Das Undbild, 1919 | Kurt Schwitters, Untitled (Chessman), 1941 | Grete Stern, Sueño No. 28: Love without Illusion, 1951 | Juan Gris, Breakfast, 1914

fields.Title: Illuminated manuscript
fields.Notes: The Book of Kells and the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry are the most famous survivors.
fields.Description: A handwritten book decorated with gold or silver, painted initials and borders, and small pictures called miniatures.
fields.Captions: Malnazar, decorated incipit page of an Armenian manuscript, 1637–38 | Vincent of Beauvais, the book's author, in a miniature made for Edward IV | Limbourg brothers, The Funeral of Raymond Diocrès, from the Très Riches Heures

fields.Title: Grisaille
fields.Notes: Often used on the closed wings of Netherlandish altarpieces, as on the Ghent Altarpiece.
fields.Description: Painting entirely in shades of grey or another neutral colour, often to imitate sculpture.
fields.Captions: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery, 1565 | Andrea del Sarto, Baptism of the People, grisaille fresco, Chiostro dello Scalzo | Grisaille wing of an altarpiece by Hans Memling

fields.Title: Fresco
fields.Notes: Buon fresco is permanent, while fresco secco, painted on dry plaster, flakes away; painters worked one day's patch, a giornata, at a time.
fields.Description: Painting with pigment in water on fresh, wet lime plaster, so that the colour dries into the wall.
fields.Captions: Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam, detail of the Sistine Chapel ceiling | Etruscan fresco | A Roman fresco of a young man from the Villa di Arianna, Stabiae, 1st century CE

fields.Title: Encaustic
fields.Notes: The medium of the Fayum mummy portraits; revived by Jasper Johns.
fields.Description: Painting in pigment suspended in hot wax, fused to the surface with heat, giving a hard durable finish.
fields.Captions: A 6th-century encaustic icon from Saint Catherine's Monastery, Egypt, depicting Peter the Apostle | Fayum mummy portrait | A modern-day encaustic painting using wax crayons, Martina Loos, 2009

fields.Title: Tempera
fields.Notes: The dominant panel medium before oil; Sandro Botticelli's The Birth of Venus is painted this way.
fields.Description: Paint bound with egg yolk, drying fast to a matte, luminous film that must be built in fine hatched strokes.
fields.Captions: Tubes of tempera paint arranged as a colour wheel | Duccio, Crevole Madonna, c. 1284, tempera and gold on wood | A tempera on wood by Niccolò Semitecolo, 1367 | Ancient Egyptian tempera wall painting of offering bearers

fields.Title: Gesso
fields.Notes: Its absorbency and brightness are what give egg-bound painting its glow.
fields.Description: The white ground of chalk or gypsum in glue brushed onto a panel and polished smooth before any paint is applied.
fields.Captions: Acrylic gesso | A restored gesso panel representing St. Martin of Tours, from St. Michael and All Angels Church, Lyndhurst, Hampshire

fields.Title: Glazing
fields.Notes: How Renaissance and Baroque painters built depth of colour; Titian worked in many such layers.
fields.Description: Laying a thin transparent film of colour over a dried layer so the one beneath shows through and alters it.
fields.Captions: Titian, Danaë, one of several versions, 1550s–60s | Titian, Bacchus and Ariadne, 1520–23 | Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring, c. 1665

fields.Title: Scumbling
fields.Notes: The opposite operation to glazing; Turner's skies depend on it.
fields.Description: Dragging a thin, broken layer of opaque light paint over a darker dry one so the under-colour glimmers through.
fields.Captions: J. M. W. Turner, Norham Castle, Sunrise, c. 1845 | J. M. W. Turner, Rain, Steam and Speed

fields.Title: Alla prima
fields.Notes: Wet-on-wet; the working method of the Impressionists and of Frans Hals before them.
fields.Description: Completing a picture in a single session while every layer is still wet, so colours mix on the surface itself.
fields.Captions: Rembrandt, Portrait of Jan Six (1654) | Winslow Homer, Rowing Home, 1890, watercolour painted wet-on-wet

fields.Title: Pentimento
fields.Notes: Italian for “repentance”; the chief evidence that a composition was reworked.
fields.Description: A change the painter made and covered, becoming visible again as the upper paint thins with age.
fields.Captions: The face of the woman in the image The Old Guitarist | Ingres, Portrait of Jacques Marquet de Norvins | Caravaggio, The Cardsharps

fields.Title: Cartoon
fields.Notes: Leonardo's Burlington House Cartoon and Raphael's cartoons for the Sistine Chapel tapestries survive.
fields.Description: A full-size preparatory drawing, its outlines pricked or incised so the design can be transferred to the final surface.
fields.Captions: Leonardo da Vinci, The Burlington House Cartoon, c. 1499–1500 | John Tenniel, Davy Jones's Locker, Punch, 1892

fields.Title: Sinopia
fields.Notes: Named for the red earth of Sinope; revealed when frescoes are detached.
fields.Description: The reddish underdrawing laid on the rough plaster of a wall to set out a composition before the final coat.
fields.Captions: A sinopia showing a king, from the Museum of Sinopie in Pisa, Italy | Sinopia underdrawing for a Madonna and Child | A sinopia for a fresco by Buonamico Buffalmacco, Museo delle Sinopie, Pisa

fields.Title: Sgraffito
fields.Notes: Used on Italian facades and on ceramics.
fields.Description: Scratching through a top layer to reveal a contrasting one beneath, in plaster, slip, or paint.
fields.Captions: Sgraffito decoration in the courtyard of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi, Florence | Palazzo Massimo Istoriato: a fading palace facade in Rome by Polidoro da Caravaggio and Maturino da Firenze, 1523 | Artist from Pedraza creates a sgraffito mural at the Casa de los Picos School of Art and Design, Segovia | Sgraffito façades, Pyrgi, Chios

fields.Title: Verdaccio
fields.Notes: Standard Florentine practice, described by Cennino Cennini; visible where the upper layers have worn.
fields.Description: A greenish-grey underpainting laid first in flesh areas, over which warm tones are worked so the shadows stay cool.
fields.Captions: Michelangelo, Manchester Madonna, National Gallery, London | A part of the Sistine Chapel ceiling painted by Michelangelo

fields.Title: Silverpoint
fields.Notes: Demands complete certainty of hand; Albrecht Dürer and Leonardo both used it.
fields.Description: Drawing with a metal stylus on a prepared coated surface, leaving a fine grey line that cannot be erased and tarnishes brown.
fields.Captions: Modern silverpoint stylus | Hans Holbein the Younger, Portrait Study of Dorothea Meyer, 1516 | Medieval stylus | William Holman Hunt, portrait of his wife Edith

fields.Title: Sanguine
fields.Notes: Red chalk; Leonardo and Jean-Antoine Watteau used it for countless figure studies.
fields.Description: Drawing in a warm red-brown chalk, favoured for studies of flesh.
fields.Captions: Leonardo da Vinci, self-portrait in red chalk, c. 1512 | Mademoiselle de Mondran, Study after a Roman Bust, 1786, red chalk

fields.Title: Woodcut
fields.Notes: The oldest European printmaking process; Albrecht Dürer's Apocalypse and Katsushika Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa are examples.
fields.Description: A relief print cut from the plank side of a block, the areas to stay white carved away so ink sits on what is left standing.
fields.Captions: Albrecht Dürer, The Four Horsemen, c. 1496–98 | Edvard Munch, The Kiss IV, woodcut, 1902

fields.Title: Wood engraving
fields.Notes: Thomas Bewick developed it; it became the standard means of illustrating 19th-century books.
fields.Description: A relief print cut with a burin into the dense end grain of a block, allowing far finer line than cutting along the plank.
fields.Captions: Thomas Bewick | Leather-covered sandbag, wood blocks, and tools (burins), used in wood engraving | The Tench, A History of British Fishes (1835), by William Yarrell

fields.Title: Linocut
fields.Notes: Taken up by Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse for its bold, flat shapes.
fields.Description: A relief print cut from soft flooring material, which offers no grain and so cuts freely in any direction.
fields.Captions: Linocut printing; using a design cut into linoleum to make a print on paper | Frank Weitzel, The Mask, 1930 | Using a handheld gouger to cut a design into linoleum for a linocut print | Ethel Spowers, Wet Afternoon, 1930, linocut

fields.Title: Engraving
fields.Notes: The most disciplined of the old processes; Albrecht Dürer and Marcantonio Raimondi are its masters.
fields.Description: An intaglio print in which lines are cut directly into a metal plate with a burin, giving a clean swelling line.
fields.Captions: St. Jerome in His Study (1514), engraving by Northern Renaissance master Albrecht Dürer | Jean-Pierre Norblin de La Gourdaine, Ecce Homo, 1774–89

fields.Title: Etching
fields.Notes: The freest of the intaglio processes because the hand draws rather than cuts; Rembrandt's are unsurpassed.
fields.Description: An intaglio print in which the plate is coated with an acid-resistant ground, drawn through with a needle and then bitten by acid.
fields.Captions: Daniel Hopfer, The Soldier and His Wife | The etched carnelian beads in this necklace from the Royal Cemetery of Ur dating to the First Dynasty of Ur | Self-portrait etched by Wenceslaus Hollar | Selection of early etched printing plates from the British Museum

fields.Title: Drypoint
fields.Notes: The burr wears away quickly, so editions are very small; Rembrandt used it for his richest late plates.
fields.Description: An intaglio print scratched straight into the plate with a hard point, the raised curl of displaced metal holding ink for a soft velvety line.
fields.Captions: Lesser Ury, Woman in a Café, drypoint | Edward Thomas Daniell, Surlingham Ferry, drypoint | Mary Cassatt, Woman Bathing, 1890–91

fields.Title: Mezzotint
fields.Notes: Capable of continuous tone without line; the great vehicle for reproducing paintings before photography.
fields.Description: An intaglio process working from dark to light: the whole plate is roughened to print solid black, then smoothed back where light is wanted.
fields.Captions: John Smith after Godfrey Kneller, Saint Agnes, mezzotint | Ludwig von Siegen, Countess Amalie Elisabeth of Hanau-Münzenberg, 1642

fields.Title: Aquatint
fields.Notes: Gives washes rather than lines; Goya combined it with etching throughout Los Caprichos.
fields.Description: An intaglio process using powdered resin melted onto the plate so acid bites around each grain, printing an even area of tone.
fields.Captions: Karl Bodmer, Indians Hunting the Bison, 1839 | Aquatint of the first production of I puritani, 1835 | Demonstration sections of printed aquatint, magnified | Goya, Los Caprichos no. 32, Por que fue sensible, 1799

fields.Title: Lithography
fields.Notes: Invented by Alois Senefelder in 1796; Honoré Daumier, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, and the poster trade lived on it.
fields.Description: A planographic process exploiting the mutual repulsion of grease and water, printing from a flat stone or plate rather than a raised or incised surface.
fields.Captions: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Moulin Rouge: La Goulue, colour lithograph poster, 1891 | Charles Marion Russell, The Custer Fight, lithograph, 1903 | A lithographic stone and the mirror-image print pulled from it

fields.Title: Screenprint
fields.Notes: Also called serigraphy; Andy Warhol made it the signature medium of Pop.
fields.Description: Forcing ink through a stretched mesh whose non-printing areas are blocked, giving flat unmodulated colour.
fields.Captions: A silkscreen printer pulling the squeegee to create a design as a demonstration of the process | A silk screen design | The poster shop at Heart Mountain War Relocation Center

fields.Title: Monotype
fields.Notes: Between painting and printmaking; Edgar Degas made hundreds.
fields.Description: An image painted onto a smooth plate and printed while wet, yielding one strong impression and at most a faint second.
fields.Captions: Monotype by Giovanni Benedetto Castiglione, probably a second impression | William Blake, Visions of the Daughters of Albion, relief etching and monotype | Edgar Degas, Brothel Scene, monotype

fields.Title: Chine-collé
fields.Notes: Used to give a warm ground under an intaglio impression.
fields.Description: Bonding a thin sheet of fine paper to a heavier support during printing, so the image sits on a different colour or texture.
fields.Captions: Chine-collé print on vellum by Eugène Delacroix, 1828 | Print on chine collé of a bookplate designed for William Corless Mills, c. 1917

fields.Title: Lost-wax casting
fields.Notes: In French cire perdue; Benvenuto Cellini described casting his Perseus with the Head of Medusa this way in his autobiography.
fields.Description: Producing a hollow bronze by modelling the form in a soft meltable material, encasing that, draining it out, and pouring metal into the void left behind.
fields.Captions: Rubber mould of a wax apple and its plaster cast | Wax model of an apple | Paraffin model of an apple | The hollow paraffin cast

fields.Title: Repoussé
fields.Notes: Its complement, chasing, refines the same form from the front. The Mask of Agamemnon is worked this way.
fields.Description: Shaping metal in relief by hammering it from the reverse so the design is pushed outward.
fields.Captions: Mask of Agamemnon, Mycenae, c. 1550–1500 BCE | The Great Dish, Mildenhall Treasure | Golden mask of Tutankhamun's mummy

fields.Title: Cloisonné
fields.Notes: The dividing wires stay visible as bright lines; Byzantine and Chinese work is celebrated.
fields.Description: Enamelling in which thin metal strips are soldered to the surface to make compartments that are then filled with coloured glass.
fields.Captions: Cloisonné enamel jar | Pectoral of Senusret II, from his daughter's grave, using shaped stones rather than enamel | Chinese Ming Dynasty cloisonné enamel bowl, using nine colours of enamel | Early 7th century Anglo-Saxon seax (knife) hilt fitting, gold with garnet cloisonné inlay

fields.Title: Champlevé
fields.Notes: The Mosan and Limoges workshops are the great medieval sources.
fields.Description: Enamelling in which hollows are gouged out of a thick metal plate and filled with glass, leaving the untouched metal as the drawing.
fields.Captions: Limoges champlevé enamel pyx, 13th century | High-quality Mosan 12th century armlet, somewhat damaged, so showing the cast recesses for the enamel | Celtic red enamel on horse-harness, Britain, c. 50 CE | The Staffordshire Moorlands Pan, 2nd century CE Romano-British

fields.Title: Mosaic
fields.Notes: The individual pieces are tesserae; glass ones backed with gold leaf give Byzantine work its light.
fields.Description: An image assembled from small cut pieces of stone or coloured glass set in mortar.
fields.Captions: Mosaic of the Emperor Justinian, San Vitale, Ravenna, c. 547 | Epiphany of Dionysus mosaic, from the Villa of Dionysus (2nd century CE) in Dion, Greece | Roman mosaic of Neptune driving sea-horses | Tragic mask, detail of an ancient Roman mosaic

fields.Title: Intarsia
fields.Notes: The studiolo at Urbino is the supreme example.
fields.Description: Inlaying shaped pieces of coloured wood into a wooden surface to form a picture, often an illusionistic one.
fields.Captions: Geometric intarsia inlaid in wood | Geometric figure (1537), intarsia by fra Damiano da Bergamo | Intarsia on the First aid kit of Alexander Karađorđević, Prince of Serbia, Historical Museum of Serbia | Domenico di Niccolò dei Cori, wooden choir of the chapel of the Palazzo Pubblico, Siena

fields.Title: Chryselephantine
fields.Notes: Phidias's lost Athena Parthenos and Statue of Zeus at Olympia were made this way.
fields.Description: Colossal sculpture built over a wooden core in gold and ivory, the flesh in ivory and the drapery in gold.
fields.Captions: Gold fittings from the chryselephantine statues found at Delphi, Archaeological Museum of Delphi | Gold and fire-blackened ivory fragments of a burnt Archaic chryselephantine statue (Delphi Archaeological Museum) | Reproduction of the Athena Parthenos in the full-scale reproduction of the Parthenon in the U.S. state of Tennessee

fields.Title: Linear perspective
fields.Notes: Demonstrated by Filippo Brunelleschi and codified by Leon Battista Alberti in De pictura (1435); Masaccio's Holy Trinity is the first great painted use.
fields.Description: A geometric system in which parallel lines receding from the viewer converge on a single point, fixing every object's size by its distance.
fields.Captions: The Ideal City, c. 1480–1490, Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, Urbino: a piazza laid out in one-point perspective | Paolo Uccello, Perspective Study of a Chalice, c. 1450, Uffizi, Florence | Albrecht Dürer, Man Drawing a Lute, 1525, from his treatise Underweysung der Messung: a thread stands in for the line of sight

fields.Title: Atmospheric perspective
fields.Notes: Also called aerial perspective; Leonardo described it and used it behind the Mona Lisa.
fields.Description: Suggesting depth by making distant things paler, bluer, and less distinct, as intervening air actually renders them.
fields.Captions: Distant ridges fading to blue: atmospheric perspective in nature | Atmospheric perspective in a landscape | Dai Jin, Landscape in the Style of Yan Wengui, early Ming dynasty

fields.Title: Foreshortening
fields.Notes: Andrea Mantegna's Lamentation of Christ is the audacious demonstration.
fields.Description: Drawing a form projecting toward the viewer as compressed along its length, so it reads as coming forward.
fields.Captions: Andrea Mantegna, Lamentation of Christ, c. 1480 | Caravaggio, Supper at Emmaus, 1601 | Caravaggio, Conversion on the Way to Damascus, 1601

fields.Title: Anamorphosis
fields.Notes: The stretched skull across the bottom of Holbein's The Ambassadors.
fields.Description: A distorted projection that resolves into a recognisable image only from one oblique angle or in a curved mirror.
fields.Captions: Example of mirror anamorphosis | Holbein's The Ambassadors with a memento mori anamorph skull in the foreground, 1533 | Two anamorphic drawings by Leonardo da Vinci, 1515

fields.Title: Divisionism
fields.Notes: The theory behind Georges Seurat's practice; the dotted variety is pointillism.
fields.Description: Placing separated strokes of pure unmixed colour side by side so the eye combines them at a distance.
fields.Captions: Georges Seurat, A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, 1884–1886 | Paul Signac, Portrait of Félix Fénéon, 1890 | Vincent van Gogh, Self-Portrait, 1887–88

fields.Title: Frottage
fields.Notes: Max Ernst's invention of 1925, from the French for “rubbing”.
fields.Description: Taking an image by laying paper over a textured surface and rubbing, then working the accidental pattern into a picture.
fields.Captions: A rubbing of portions of a book cover | Visitors to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial make rubbings of names | Coin image using the frottage technique

fields.Title: Decalcomania
fields.Notes: Oscar Domínguez devised it in 1936, and Max Ernst used it to generate forms without deciding them.
fields.Description: Pressing paint between two surfaces and pulling them apart, letting chance produce a blotted, veined texture.
fields.Captions: H. Grobe, Fire & Ice, 1975 | Jindřich Štyrský, decalcomania, 1936 | A modern decalcomania: paint pressed between two surfaces and pulled apart

fields.Title: Grattage
fields.Notes: The scraped counterpart of frottage; another Surrealist device of Max Ernst's.
fields.Description: Scraping wet paint off the canvas, often over a textured object beneath, to reveal what lies under.
fields.Captions: Giovanni Guida, Apotheosis of Dante Alighieri in Florence, 2020, grattage | Giovanni Guida, Apotheosis, 2014, grattage

fields.Title: Automatism
fields.Notes: Borrowed from psychoanalysis; the founding Surrealist method, seen in André Masson's automatic drawings, and an ancestor of gestural abstraction.
fields.Description: Working without conscious control so that the hand produces marks the mind has not planned.
fields.Captions: André Masson, Automatic Drawing, 1924 | Guillaume Apollinaire, La cravate et la montre, calligram from Calligrammes, 1918

fields.Title: Assemblage
fields.Notes: The sculptural counterpart of collage; Robert Rauschenberg called his hybrids Combines.
fields.Description: Building a work in three dimensions from found objects and fragments rather than carving or modelling.
fields.Captions: Kurt Schwitters, Merz 1925, 1. Relief in the Blue Square, 1925 | Jeff Wassmann, Vorwärts!, 2003 | John Chamberlain, S, 1959, metal | Werner Stürenburg, Assemblage No. 5, 1968

fields.Title: Readymade
fields.Notes: Marcel Duchamp's Fountain and Bicycle Wheel; the founding gesture of conceptual practice.
fields.Description: Designating an unaltered manufactured object as a work of art by selection alone.
fields.Captions: Marcel Duchamp, Bicycle Wheel, 1913 (later replica) | Marcel Duchamp, Fountain, 1917

fields.Title: Papier collé
fields.Notes: Georges Braque's introduction of it in 1912 opened Synthetic Cubism.
fields.Description: Pasting cut paper -- newsprint, wallpaper, labels -- onto a drawing or canvas as part of the composition.
fields.Captions: Georges Braque, Fruit Dish and Glass, 1912 | Juan Gris, Breakfast, 1914

fields.Title: Triptych
fields.Notes: The standard altarpiece format; Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights is one.
fields.Description: A picture in three hinged panels, the outer two often folding over the centre.
fields.Captions: Peter Paul Rubens, The Elevation of the Cross, 1610–11, Antwerp Cathedral | Akseli Gallen-Kallela, The Aino Myth, 1891 | Giotto, Stefaneschi Triptych, c. 1315–20 | Hieronymus Bosch, The Garden of Earthly Delights, 1490–1510

fields.Title: Diptych
fields.Notes: The Wilton Diptych is the celebrated English example.
fields.Description: A work in two hinged panels of equal size.
fields.Captions: Ivory consular diptych of Areobindus, Byzantium, 506 CE, Louvre | Wax tablet and a Roman stylus | The Barberini Ivory, Constantinople, 6th century, Louvre | Diptych with the Coronation of the Virgin and the Last Judgment, Metropolitan Museum of Art

fields.Title: Polyptych
fields.Notes: The Ghent Altarpiece of Hubert and Jan van Eyck is the great example.
fields.Description: An altarpiece of more than three panels, often in tiers with a predella below.
fields.Captions: Lamb of God Annunciation | Jan and Hubert van Eyck, Ghent Altarpiece (closed), 1432 | Polyptych with Coronation of the Virgin and Saints by Cenni di Francesco, 1390s | Duccio, Polyptych no. 47, 1315–19

fields.Title: Predella
fields.Notes: Usually recounts the life of the saint shown above.
fields.Description: The horizontal strip of small narrative scenes running along the base of an altarpiece.
fields.Captions: Predella with Saint Anne, the Virgin, and Child, on a parish-church high altar, Luxembourg | Altarpiece by Carlo Crivelli, 1468 | Altarpiece with carved and painted predella at Marienkirche Stralsund, Germany | Flemish altarpiece of the 1550s, still with three predella scenes

fields.Title: Tondo
fields.Notes: A Florentine speciality; Michelangelo's Doni Tondo and Raphael's Alba Madonna are examples.
fields.Description: A painting or relief made in a circular format.
fields.Captions: Fra Angelico and Filippo Lippi, The Adoration of the Magi, c. 1440–1460 | Glazed terracotta tondo from the della Robbia workshop | Sandro Botticelli, Madonna of the Pomegranate, c. 1487 | Michelangelo, Taddei Tondo, c. 1504–1506

fields.Title: Vanitas
fields.Notes: A Dutch speciality of the 17th century and a subset of memento mori; Pieter Claesz and Harmen Steenwyck were its masters.
fields.Description: A still life whose objects -- skull, snuffed candle, cut flowers, watch -- are assembled to insist that life is short.
fields.Captions: Pieter Claesz, Vanitas Still Life, 1630 | Antonio de Pereda, Vanitas | Vanitas by Bartholomaeus Bruyn the Elder (1524) with the text “Omnia morte cadunt, mors ultima linea rerum”

fields.Title: Memento mori
fields.Notes: Latin for “remember that you must die”; the skull is its commonest form.
fields.Description: Any image included to remind the viewer of death.
fields.Captions: Replica of a Dance of Death fresco | Unshrouded skeleton on Diana Warburton's tomb (dated 1693) in St John the Baptist Church, Chester

fields.Title: Odalisque
fields.Notes: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres's Grande Odalisque and Henri Matisse's series of odalisques.
fields.Description: A reclining female nude presented as an inhabitant of a harem, a staple of European orientalist painting.
fields.Captions: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Odalisque, 1870 | Marià Fortuny's The Odalisque (1861) | Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, Grande Odalisque, 1814 | Jules Joseph Lefebvre, Odalisque, 1874

fields.Title: Pietà
fields.Notes: Michelangelo's in Saint Peter's is the most famous of many.
fields.Description: A depiction of the Virgin seated with the dead Christ across her lap.
fields.Captions: Giovanni Bellini, Pietà, c. 1505 | Michelangelo, Pietà, 1498–99, Saint Peter's Basilica | Pietà sculpture, Salzburg, 1470s | Pietà as Our Lady of Charity, Cartagena, 1723

fields.Title: Kouros
fields.Notes: The female counterpart, draped, is a kore; both precede the relaxed stance of classical sculpture.
fields.Description: An Archaic Greek standing male nude, rigidly frontal with one foot advanced and hands at the sides.
fields.Captions: An Archaic Greek kouros | The Kroisos Kouros, c. 530 BCE | Kleobis and Biton, c. 580 BCE, Delphi Archaeological Museum | Saite sculpture from the Egyptian 26th dynasty, similar in proportion and form to the early kouros type, Louvre

fields.Title: Baroque
fields.Artist: Caravaggio; Peter Paul Rubens; Gian Lorenzo Bernini; Diego Velázquez
fields.Notes: The visual arm of the Counter-Reformation and of Europe's absolutist courts.
fields.Description: A 17th-century manner of dramatic diagonals, theatrical light, and emotional immediacy, made to move the viewer.
fields.Captions: Villa Doria Pamphili, Rome | Peter Paul Rubens, Venus and Adonis | Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Ecstasy of Saint Teresa | The Marble Courtyard, Palace of Versailles

fields.Title: Northern Renaissance
fields.Artist: Jan van Eyck; Rogier van der Weyden; Hieronymus Bosch; Pieter Bruegel the Elder; Albrecht Dürer
fields.Notes: The Ghent Altarpiece (1432) and the Arnolfini Portrait (1434) are early landmarks of its oil technique.
fields.Description: The 15th- and 16th-century flowering north of the Alps, marked by oil technique, minute detail, and disguised symbolism rather than classical revival.
fields.Captions: The Adoration of the Magi in the snow, Pieter Brueghel the Younger, 1584–1638 | Jan van Eyck, The Arnolfini Portrait, 1434, National Gallery, London | Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man, c. 1490

fields.Title: Barbizon School
fields.Artist: Théodore Rousseau; Jean-François Millet; Camille Corot; Charles-François Daubigny
fields.Notes: Named for the village near Fontainebleau; the immediate ancestor of Impressionism.
fields.Description: A group of French painters who left the studio to work directly from the forest and fields, treating landscape as a subject in its own right.
fields.Captions: Camille Corot, Road by the Water, c. 1865–70 | Charles-François Daubigny, The Pond at Gylieu, 1853 | Théodore Rousseau, Becquigny, c. 1857

fields.Title: Nabis
fields.Artist: Pierre Bonnard; Édouard Vuillard; Maurice Denis; Paul Sérusier
fields.Notes: The name is Hebrew for “prophets”; The Talisman (1888), painted under Paul Gauguin's guidance, was their founding picture.
fields.Description: A group working in flat decorative colour and heavy outline, treating the picture as a surface before it is a window.
fields.Captions: Paul Sérusier, The Talisman, 1888, the first Nabi painting | Maurice Denis, Motif romanesque, 1890 | Pierre Bonnard, Woman in a Polka-Dot Dress, from Women in the Garden, 1890–91 | Pierre Bonnard, Woman with a Cape, from Women in the Garden, 1890–91

fields.Title: Der Blaue Reiter
fields.Artist: Wassily Kandinsky; Franz Marc; August Macke; Paul Klee
fields.Notes: Founded in Munich in 1911 and named after its almanac; it ended with the First World War.
fields.Description: A German group pursuing spiritual expression through colour and moving toward pure abstraction.
fields.Captions: Wassily Kandinsky, The Blue Rider, 1903 | Franz Marc, Blue Horse I, 1911 | Franz Marc, The Tower of Blue Horses, 1913 (missing since 1945)

fields.Title: Die Brücke
fields.Artist: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner; Erich Heckel; Karl Schmidt-Rottluff; Emil Nolde
fields.Notes: Founded by four architecture students in Dresden in 1905; the name means “The Bridge”.
fields.Description: A German group of harsh angular forms, clashing colour, and revived woodcut, seeking directness against academic polish.
fields.Captions: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, poster for a Brücke exhibition, 1910 | Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, A Group of Artists, 1926–27

fields.Title: Precisionism
fields.Artist: Charles Sheeler; Charles Demuth; Georgia O'Keeffe
fields.Notes: Sometimes called Cubist-Realism; My Egypt (1927) turned a grain elevator into a monument.
fields.Description: An American manner rendering factories, grain elevators, and bridges in clean geometry and smooth surfaces.
fields.Captions: Charles Demuth, Aucassin and Nicolette, oil on canvas, 1921 | Charles Demuth, I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold, 1928, Metropolitan Museum of Art | Paul Strand, Wall Street, 1915 | Morton Livingston Schamberg, Telephone, 1916

fields.Title: Regionalism
fields.Artist: Grant Wood; Thomas Hart Benton; John Steuart Curry
fields.Notes: American Gothic (1930) is its best-known picture; it turned from European modernism to the American heartland.
fields.Description: An American movement of the 1930s depicting rural Midwestern life in a deliberately plain, legible style.
fields.Captions: Grant Wood, The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere, 1931 | Thomas Hart Benton, People of Chilmark, 1920 | John Steuart Curry, Tragic Prelude, 1938–1940

fields.Title: Harlem Renaissance
fields.Artist: Aaron Douglas; Augusta Savage; Jacob Lawrence
fields.Notes: In letters its voices were Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, and Claude McKay; Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925) was its manifesto.
fields.Description: The flowering of African American art and letters centred on one New York neighbourhood between the wars.
fields.Captions: Three women in Harlem during the Harlem Renaissance | Adelaide Hall and Bill “Bojangles” Robinson in Brown Buddies, 1930

fields.Title: Art Informel
fields.Artist: Jean Fautrier; Wols; Jean Dubuffet; Hans Hartung
fields.Notes: Tachisme and art brut belong to its orbit; the critic Michel Tapié named it in the early 1950s.
fields.Description: A postwar European tendency toward improvised, gestural, and matter-laden abstraction rejecting geometric order.
fields.Captions: Painting by Laurent Jiménez-Balaguer | Jean Dubuffet, Soul of the Underground, 1959

fields.Title: Color Field painting
fields.Artist: Mark Rothko; Barnett Newman; Clyfford Still; Helen Frankenthaler
fields.Notes: An offshoot of Abstract Expressionism; a later generation stained thinned paint straight into raw canvas.
fields.Description: Abstraction built from large uninterrupted expanses of colour, seeking an immediate enveloping effect rather than gesture.
fields.Captions: Claudia Desgranges, Composite Painting, Munich Painting No. 2, 2019 | Henri Matisse, View of Notre-Dame, 1914

fields.Title: Op art
fields.Notes: Named in 1964 and brought to wide notice by MoMA's 1965 exhibition The Responsive Eye.
fields.Description: Abstraction constructed to produce optical effects -- vibration, flicker, and apparent movement -- in the viewer's eye.
fields.Captions: Victor Vasarely, Sign sculpture after Tridim-Q, Pécs, 1977 | Yaacov Agam, Fire and Water Fountain, Tel Aviv | Francis Picabia, Optophone I, c. 1921–22 | Jesús Soto, Caracas (1996)

fields.Title: Arte Povera
fields.Artist: Michelangelo Pistoletto; Mario Merz; Jannis Kounellis; Giovanni Anselmo
fields.Notes: Named by the critic Germano Celant in 1967; Venus of the Rags is its best-known work.
fields.Description: An Italian tendency using humble and untreated materials -- earth, rags, twigs, rope -- against the polish of commercial art.
fields.Captions: Mario Merz, Igloo, Kröller-Müller Museum | Giovanni Anselmo, Torsion, 1968

fields.Title: Land art
fields.Artist: Robert Smithson; Michael Heizer; Walter De Maria; Nancy Holt
fields.Notes: Landmarks include Spiral Jetty, The Lightning Field, Double Negative, and Sun Tunnels.
fields.Description: Work made by shaping the landscape itself, sited far from galleries and often known chiefly through photographs.
fields.Captions: Spiral Jetty by Robert Smithson, Rozel Point, Utah, in March 2016 | Sun Tunnels by Nancy Holt in Utah | Museum paper board left on the bank of the river for 4 days

fields.Title: Fluxus
fields.Artist: George Maciunas; Yoko Ono; Nam June Paik; Joseph Beuys
fields.Notes: Named in 1961 from the Latin for “flow”; John Cage's composition classes were a formative influence.
fields.Description: An international network favouring events, instructions, and everyday actions over permanent objects.
fields.Captions: Fluxus performers on stage, 1960s | Yoko Ono, Cut Piece, 1964 | Philip Corner, Piano Activities, Fluxus Festival, Wiesbaden, 1962

fields.Title: Neo-expressionism
fields.Location: Germany, Italy, and the United States
fields.Artist: Georg Baselitz; Anselm Kiefer; Jean-Michel Basquiat; Julian Schnabel
fields.Notes: Called Neue Wilde in Germany and Transavanguardia in Italy; its market boom peaked in the early 1980s.
fields.Description: A return in the late 1970s to large, roughly worked figurative painting after a decade of conceptual and minimal work.
fields.Captions: Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Skull), 1981 | Eric Fischl, Bad Boy, 1981

fields.Title: Photorealism
fields.Artist: Chuck Close; Richard Estes; Audrey Flack; Ralph Goings
fields.Notes: Typical subjects were monumental heads, gleaming shopfronts, diners, and cars.
fields.Description: Painting worked from photographs to reproduce their detail and optical character exactly.
fields.Captions: John Baeder, John's Diner with John's Chevelle, 2007 | Magda Torres Gurza, La hora del té

fields.Title: Social realism
fields.Notes: Distinct from the state-mandated Socialist Realism of the USSR.
fields.Description: Art depicting the conditions of working people and the poor with an explicitly critical purpose.
fields.Captions: Grant Wood, American Gothic, 1930 | Charles de Groux, The Blessing, 1860 | Jacob Riis, Bandit's Roost, 1888, from How the Other Half Lives | Gustave Courbet, A Burial at Ornans, 1849–50

fields.Title: Vienna Secession
fields.Artist: Gustav Klimt; Koloman Moser; Joseph Maria Olbrich; Josef Hoffmann
fields.Notes: Its motto: “To every age its art, to art its freedom”; the Beethoven Frieze was made for its 1902 exhibition.
fields.Description: An Austrian group that broke from the academy to pursue a total decorative art of pattern, gold, and symbolic subject.
fields.Captions: The Secession Building, Vienna, Joseph Maria Olbrich, 1898 | Secession 2016, Vienna | Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze, 1902 | Secession Group in Vienna (1902)

fields.Title: Fête galante
fields.Artist: Jean-Antoine Watteau; Nicolas Lancret; Jean-Baptiste Pater
fields.Notes: The French Academy created the category in 1717 to accept The Embarkation for Cythera.
fields.Description: An early 18th-century French subject: elegant figures at leisure in a parkland setting, wistful rather than boisterous.
fields.Captions: Antoine Watteau, Embarkation for Cythera, 1717 | Antoine Watteau, Fêtes vénitiennes, 1718–19 | Antoine Watteau, Mezzetin, c. 1718–1720 | Nicolas Lancret, Le Moulinet, c. 1730

fields.Title: Academic art
fields.Artist: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres; Alexandre Cabanel; William-Adolphe Bouguereau; Jean-Léon Gérôme
fields.Notes: Enforced through the Salon, whose juries the Impressionists gave up on after the Salon des Refusés of 1863; French detractors later called its practitioners pompiers.
fields.Description: Highly finished painting made to the rules taught by the official European art schools, which ranked scripture, myth, and history above landscape or still life and put drawing before colour.
fields.Captions: Alexandre Cabanel, The Birth of Venus, 1863 | Carlo Maratti, The Academy of Drawing, c. 1704–09 | Charles Le Brun, The Apotheosis of Louis XIV, 1677

fields.Title: Action painting
fields.Artist: Jackson Pollock; Willem de Kooning; Franz Kline
fields.Notes: Harold Rosenberg named it in a 1952 essay, calling the canvas “an arena in which to act” rather than a surface on which to reproduce something.
fields.Description: The gestural wing of Abstract Expressionism, in which dripping, flinging, and slashing pigment made the physical event of making the picture its real subject.
fields.Captions: Sabra, 1956, Berardo Collection, Lisbon | Gouache study for a mural, commissioned by the WPA, 1940 | De Kooning in front of one of his works (Amsterdam, 1968) | Pollock in 1928

fields.Title: American Impressionism
fields.Artist: Childe Hassam; John Henry Twachtman; Theodore Robinson; William Merritt Chase
fields.Notes: The Ten broke from the Society of American Artists in 1897 to exhibit together; Theodore Robinson worked beside Monet at Giverny.
fields.Description: A United States adaptation of French plein-air painting, brought home by artists who had trained in Paris and then gathered in summer colonies such as Old Lyme, Cos Cob, and Giverny.
fields.Captions: An American plein-air painting of the 1890s | Frank W. Benson, Eleanor Holding a Shell, North Haven, Maine, 1902 | Theodore Robinson, Low Tide, Riverside Yacht Club, 1894 | Mary Cassatt, The Child's Bath, 1893

fields.Title: Analytic Cubism
fields.Notes: Succeeded by the Synthetic phase, which brought back bright colour, pasted paper, and legible signs; the Portrait of Ambroise Vollard (1910) is a standard example.
fields.Description: The first, austere phase of its movement: objects taken apart into shifting facets seen from several viewpoints at once, in a palette narrowed almost to grey, ochre, and brown.
fields.Captions: Pablo Picasso, Girl with a Mandolin, 1910 | Fernand Léger, Nudes in the Forest, 1909–11

fields.Title: Art Nouveau
fields.Artist: Alphonse Mucha; Hector Guimard; Victor Horta; Louis Comfort Tiffany
fields.Notes: Named after Siegfried Bing's Paris shop; the same style went by Jugendstil in Germany, Modernisme in Catalonia, Stile Liberty in Italy, and Sezessionstil in Vienna.
fields.Description: An international decorative style of whiplash curves and forms taken from plants, insects, and streaming hair, applied alike to buildings, glass, jewellery, and posters.
fields.Captions: Hector Guimard, a Paris Métro entrance | Alphonse Mucha, poster for Job cigarette papers, 1896 | Tiffany Studios, Wisteria table lamp, c. 1901 | Victor Horta, the stair hall of the Hôtel Tassel, Brussels, 1893

fields.Title: Ashcan School
fields.Artist: Robert Henri; John Sloan; George Bellows; George Luks
fields.Notes: Grew out of Robert Henri's circle, eight of whom exhibited together in 1908 as The Eight; the name was a later jibe at the group's subject matter.
fields.Description: An early 20th-century New York group that gave up genteel subjects for tenements, saloons, boxing matches, and crowded pavements, painted in dark, rapid strokes.
fields.Captions: John Sloan, McSorley's Bar, 1912 | Ashcan School artists and friends at John French Sloan's Philadelphia studio, 1898

fields.Title: Berlin Secession
fields.Artist: Max Liebermann; Lovis Corinth; Max Slevogt; Käthe Kollwitz
fields.Notes: Emil Nolde's 1910 attack on Liebermann in print led the younger members to break away as the New Secession; Paul Cassirer's gallery was the commercial arm.
fields.Description: A German artists' association founded in 1898 under Max Liebermann, after the official salon jury threw out a Walter Leistikow landscape, giving Impressionist and then Expressionist painters their own exhibitions.
fields.Captions: A Secession gathering drawn from life | Jury for the Berlin Secession 1908 exhibition. | Edvard Munch, The Dance of Life, 1899–1900 | Building of the Berlin Secession in Tiergartenstraße 21a

fields.Title: Biedermeier
fields.Artist: Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller; Carl Spitzweg; Friedrich von Amerling
fields.Notes: Named after Gottlieb Biedermaier, a fictional provincial schoolmaster-poet invented for a Munich comic magazine in the 1850s.
fields.Description: The middle-class art of central Europe between the Congress of Vienna and the revolutions of 1848: small, tidy, brightly lit pictures of domestic contentment, with plain veneered furniture to match.
fields.Captions: A central European genre landscape of the 1830s | Austrian Biedermeier sofa, c. 1815–1825, mahogany, upholstery (not original), Montreal Museum of Fine Arts (Montreal, Canada) | Emperor Francis I of Austria in his study at the Hofburg Palace. | Biedermeier room in the museum of Chrzanów, Poland

fields.Title: Body art
fields.Artist: Marina Abramović; Chris Burden; Vito Acconci; Carolee Schneemann
fields.Notes: Chris Burden had himself shot in the arm for Shoot (1971); Abramović laid out 72 objects, a loaded pistol among them, for the audience to use on her in Rhythm 0 (1974).
fields.Description: A tendency of the 1960s and 1970s in which the artist's own flesh is the material worked on -- cut, endured, exposed or put at real risk in front of an audience.
fields.Captions: Marina Abramović, The Artist Is Present, MoMA, 2010 | Body painting | Russian avantgarde painter Natalia Goncharova during her 1913 performance.

fields.Title: Bolognese School
fields.Artist: Annibale Carracci; Ludovico Carracci; Guido Reni; Guercino; Domenichino
fields.Notes: Its Accademia degli Incamminati was the model for later art academies; Annibale Carracci's Farnese Gallery ceiling in Rome is its landmark.
fields.Description: The academy three Carracci cousins founded and the painters it trained, who answered Mannerist artifice with life drawing, clear composition, and a return to Raphael and the Venetians.
fields.Captions: Annibale Carracci, from the Farnese Gallery ceiling | Portrait likely to be of Isabella d'Este, attributed to Francesco Francia, 1511 | Prospero Fontana, Deposition of Christ, 1563 | Domenichino, Saint Cecilia Distributing Alms, 1612–15, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome

fields.Title: Caravaggisti
fields.Artist: Bartolomeo Manfredi; Orazio Gentileschi; Artemisia Gentileschi; Jusepe de Ribera; Valentin de Boulogne
fields.Notes: Bartolomeo Manfredi's version -- tavern scenes of card sharps, fortune tellers, and musicians -- was imitated so widely that it was known as the manfrediana methodus.
fields.Description: The European painters who took up one Roman master's violent single-source light, cropped half-length figures, and unidealized models, carrying his manner to Naples, Utrecht, Spain, and France.
fields.Captions: A tenebrist martyrdom by a follower of Caravaggio | Bartolomeo Manfredi, Mars Chastising Cupid, c. 1605–10 | Peter Paul Rubens, Cain Slaying Abel, 1608–09

fields.Title: Utrecht Caravaggisti
fields.Artist: Hendrick ter Brugghen; Gerard van Honthorst; Dirck van Baburen
fields.Notes: Gerard van Honthorst's night scenes earned him the Italian nickname Gherardo delle Notti; Baburen's The Procuress hangs on the wall inside two of Vermeer's paintings.
fields.Description: Three Dutch Catholic painters who studied in Rome and brought its candlelit, half-length tavern and musician scenes home, where their lighting fed into Vermeer and the young Rembrandt.
fields.Captions: A candlelit musician scene in the Utrecht manner | Gerard van Honthorst, The Procuress, 1625 | Hendrick ter Brugghen, Bacchante with an Ape, 1627 | Dirck van Baburen, The Crowning with Thorns, 1622

fields.Title: Classical antiquity
fields.Notes: Its sculpture is divided into Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic phases, and most Greek bronzes survive only as Roman marble copies.
fields.Description: The Greek and Roman world whose sculpture, architecture, and painting set the standard that European art kept returning to -- in the Carolingian revival, the Renaissance, and again in the 18th century.
fields.Captions: The Doryphoros of Polykleitos, Roman copy, Naples | Hades abducting Persephone, 4th-century BCE wall painting in the small Macedonian royal tomb at Vergina

fields.Title: Cloisonnism
fields.Artist: Émile Bernard; Louis Anquetin; Paul Gauguin
fields.Notes: The critic Édouard Dujardin coined the name in 1888 for Louis Anquetin's work; Gauguin's Vision after the Sermon is the best-known painting in the manner.
fields.Description: Painting in flat areas of strong unmodelled colour fenced in by dark outlines, named for the metalworking process whose soldered wire partitions the outlines resemble.
fields.Captions: Paul Gauguin, The Yellow Christ, 1889 | Paul Gauguin, The Yellow Christ, 1889 | Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Portrait of Émile Bernard, 1886 | Autoportrait à la pipe, 1892

fields.Title: CoBrA
fields.Artist: Asger Jorn; Karel Appel; Constant Nieuwenhuys; Christian Dotremont
fields.Notes: Its name is an acronym of its members' three home cities -- Copenhagen, Brussels, Amsterdam; it dissolved in 1951 after two exhibitions and fed into Situationism.
fields.Description: A short-lived postwar northern European group whose violent, brightly coloured, half-childish figures were drawn from children's drawing, folk art, and Nordic myth, in revolt against both Socialist Realism and geometric abstraction.
fields.Captions: Karel Appel, Saut dans l'espace, 1953 | Pierre Alechinsky, Le Bruit de la chute, 1974–75 | Karel Appel, Frog with Umbrella, 2001, the Spui, The Hague | Karel Appel, The Elephant, University of Maryland

fields.Title: Cubo-Futurism
fields.Artist: Kazimir Malevich; Natalia Goncharova; Lyubov Popova; Olga Rozanova
fields.Notes: Its poets, Mayakovsky and Khlebnikov among them, staged the zaum opera Victory over the Sun (1913), whose sets led Malevich to Suprematism.
fields.Description: The Russian fusion of French faceting with Italian machine dynamism, building peasants and townspeople out of gleaming metallic cones and cylinders.
fields.Captions: Natalia Goncharova, The Cyclist, 1913 | Natalia Goncharova, The Cyclist, 1913, State Russian Museum | Dmitry Melnikov, Portrait of Sergei Shchukin, 1915

fields.Title: Delft School
fields.Artist: Johannes Vermeer; Pieter de Hooch; Carel Fabritius; Gerard Houckgeest
fields.Notes: Carel Fabritius, Rembrandt's most gifted pupil, was killed in the 1654 gunpowder explosion that destroyed much of the town and most of his work.
fields.Description: The painters of one Dutch pottery town, known for silent sunlit interiors, precisely measured perspective, church views, and townscapes of the place itself.
fields.Captions: Interiors and town views by the painters of Delft | Carel Fabritius, A View of Delft, 1652 | Johannes Vermeer, The Milkmaid, c. 1657–58

fields.Title: Düsseldorf School
fields.Artist: Wilhelm von Schadow; Andreas Achenbach; Emanuel Leutze; Albert Bierstadt
fields.Notes: Emanuel Leutze painted Washington Crossing the Delaware there; Albert Bierstadt and Worthington Whittredge carried the manner into the Hudson River School.
fields.Description: One German academy's circle of landscape and history painters, whose crisp detail and dramatic weather shaped a generation of American painters who went there to train.
fields.Captions: Andreas Achenbach, an Italian landscape | Andreas Achenbach, The Old Academy in Düsseldorf, 1831 | Andreas Achenbach, Clearing Up—Coast of Sicily, 1847, Walters Art Museum | George Caleb Bingham, Jolly Flatboatmen in Port, 1857

fields.Title: Dutch Golden Age
fields.Artist: Rembrandt van Rijn; Johannes Vermeer; Frans Hals; Jacob van Ruisdael
fields.Notes: Painters specialized narrowly by subject, and output was large enough that pictures hung in ordinary houses; the tulip trade and the East India Company paid for much of it.
fields.Description: The 17th century in a newly independent Protestant republic, where a merchant public with no church commissions to give bought small pictures of landscape, still life, seascape, and daily life instead.
fields.Captions: Johannes Vermeer, The Milkmaid, c. 1658 | Frans Hals, Gypsy Girl, 1628–30 | Rembrandt, The Blinding of Samson, 1636

fields.Title: Feminist art
fields.Artist: Judy Chicago; Miriam Schapiro; Barbara Kruger; Guerrilla Girls
fields.Notes: Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party (1979) lays 39 places for historical women; the Guerrilla Girls' 1989 poster asked whether women had to be naked to get into the Met.
fields.Description: Work from the 1960s onward that set out to expose how women had been shut out of the canon and confined to craft, often reclaiming needlework, china painting, and the body itself as materials.
fields.Captions: Judy Chicago, The Dinner Party, 1979 | Womanhouse, by Judy Chicago, Miriam Schapiro, and their students, Los Angeles, 1972 | Sheila de Bretteville, Pink, poster, 1973 | Sutapa Biswas

fields.Title: Gothic
fields.Notes: Named as an insult by Renaissance Italians who blamed the style on the barbarians who had sacked Rome; Vasari popularized the slur.
fields.Description: The art of later medieval Europe, its painting and sculpture growing more slender, swaying and naturalistic alongside the pointed-arch cathedrals it was made for.
fields.Captions: Jamb figures from the west front of Chartres Cathedral | Mary Magdalene, International Gothic, 14th century, St. John's Cathedral, Toruń

fields.Title: Graffiti
fields.Artist: Jean-Michel Basquiat; Keith Haring; Futura 2000; Lee Quiñones
fields.Notes: TAKI 183's tags drew a New York Times article in 1971; Basquiat began as SAMO, and Haring drew in chalk on the blank black paper of unsold subway advertising panels.
fields.Description: Spray-painted names and figures put up illegally on subway cars and walls in 1970s New York, which dealers moved into galleries within a decade.
fields.Captions: A trackside wall of spray-painted tags | A graffito caricature of a politician, Villa of the Mysteries, Pompeii | Figure graffito, similar to a relief, at the Castellania, in Valletta

fields.Title: Group of Seven
fields.Artist: Lawren Harris; A. Y. Jackson; Arthur Lismer; Frederick Varley
fields.Notes: Tom Thomson, who painted The Jack Pine, drowned in 1917 before it formed; Emily Carr exhibited alongside it without joining, and it became the Canadian Group of Painters in 1933.
fields.Description: Canadian landscape painters who set out after the First World War to paint the northern wilderness of their own country in bold, flat, brilliant colour instead of in a European manner.
fields.Captions: Lawren Harris, North Shore, Lake Superior, 1926 | The group at the Arts and Letters Club, Toronto, about 1920 | Frederick Varley, Gas Chamber at Seaford, 1918, Canadian War Museum, Ottawa | Tom Thomson, The Jack Pine, 1916–17, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa

fields.Title: Hague School
fields.Artist: Jozef Israëls; Anton Mauve; Jacob Maris; Willem Maris
fields.Notes: Critics called them the Grey School for that palette; Anton Mauve was Van Gogh's cousin by marriage and his first teacher in oils.
fields.Description: Dutch painters of grey skies, wet beaches, polders, and peasant labour, working in a subdued tonal palette that revived their own 17th-century landscape tradition.
fields.Captions: Anton Mauve, horsemen on a Dutch beach | Wijnand Nuyen, Shipwreck on a Rocky Coast, 1828–39 | Jan Hendrik Weissenbruch, Forest View near Barbizon, 1900 | Gerard Bilders, Cows at a Pond

fields.Title: Hellenistic
fields.Location: Greece, Egypt and the Near East
fields.Notes: Laocoön and His Sons, the Winged Victory of Samothrace, the Dying Gaul and the Pergamon Altar frieze are its monuments.
fields.Description: The Greek art made between Alexander's death and the Roman conquest, which traded Classical restraint for violent movement, extreme emotion, old age, pain, and deep spiralling compositions.
fields.Captions: The Winged Victory of Samothrace, c. 190 BCE | A scene from the Alexander Sarcophagus | The Barberini Faun, a Hellenistic marble of the 2nd century BCE or a Roman copy of an earlier bronze | Ludovisi Gaul, Roman copy of a Hellenistic original, Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome

fields.Title: Hyperrealism
fields.Artist: Chuck Close; Richard Estes; Ron Mueck; Duane Hanson
fields.Notes: Grew out of Photorealism but pushes past it into an unsettling literalism; Ron Mueck's figures keep every skin detail while changing scale.
fields.Description: Painting and sculpture finished to a pitch of detail beyond what a photograph records -- pores, stubble, single hairs, reflections -- so that the result looks more sharply present than life.
fields.Captions: A cast figure finished to beyond photographic detail | Duane Hanson, Woman Eating, polyester resin and fibreglass, Smithsonian American Art Museum | Charles Bell, Circus Act, screenprint, 1995 | Magda Torres Gurza, La hora del té

fields.Title: Installation art
fields.Artist: Yayoi Kusama; Ilya Kabakov; Olafur Eliasson; Judy Chicago
fields.Notes: Kusama's mirrored Infinity Rooms and Olafur Eliasson's The Weather Project in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall are the crowd-drawing examples.
fields.Description: Work built for one room and one occasion, which the viewer walks into and is surrounded by rather than standing in front of.
fields.Captions: Olafur Eliasson, The Weather Project, Tate Modern, 2003–2004 | Yayoi Kusama, The Obliteration Room, first shown 2002 | Judy Chicago, The Dinner Party, 1974–1979: Sappho's place setting | Menashe Kadishman, Shalechet (Fallen Leaves), Jewish Museum Berlin

fields.Title: Jack of Diamonds
fields.Artist: Pyotr Konchalovsky; Ilya Mashkov; Aristarkh Lentulov; Robert Falk
fields.Notes: Larionov and Goncharova walked out in 1912 to found the cruder, more folk-rooted Donkey's Tail.
fields.Description: A Moscow exhibiting society founded in 1910 and named, deliberately, after a playing card that Russian slang attached to convicts; its members painted Russian subjects in bright Cézannesque and Fauve colour.
fields.Captions: A Moscow figure painting in Fauve colour, c. 1913 | Aristarkh Lentulov, Woman with a Guitar, 1913 | Aristarkh Lentulov, Saint Basil's Cathedral, 1913, Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow | Portrait of the Artist's Family, 1911

fields.Title: Jugendstil
fields.Artist: Hermann Obrist; August Endell; Otto Eckmann; Peter Behrens
fields.Notes: The magazine was Die Jugend (“Youth”), founded in 1896; Peter Behrens passed through it on the way to designing for AEG.
fields.Description: The German form of Art Nouveau, named after a Munich magazine, moving from floral whiplash ornament towards a harder, more geometric line by about 1900.
fields.Captions: Joseph Maria Olbrich, the Secession Building, Vienna | Lovis Corinth, Portrait of Otto Eckmann | Hermann Obrist, Krupp Fountain, 1912, Munich | A simplified version of Hermann Obrist's Cyclamen

fields.Title: Les XX
fields.Artist: James Ensor; Théo van Rysselberghe; Fernand Khnopff; Octave Maus
fields.Notes: Octave Maus ran it and its successor, La Libre Esthétique; Anna Boch bought Van Gogh's The Red Vineyard out of its 1890 salon.
fields.Description: A Brussels society of twenty artists that held ten annual salons, inviting Seurat, Van Gogh, Gauguin, and Cézanne to Belgium years before Paris would have them.
fields.Captions: James Ensor, Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889 | Claude Monet, La Manneporte, Étretat, 1886 | James Ensor in front of Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889 in his house in Ostend, 1940s | James Ensor, Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889, 1888, Getty Museum

fields.Title: Luminism
fields.Artist: Fitz Henry Lane; Martin Johnson Heade; John Frederick Kensett; Sanford Robinson Gifford
fields.Notes: The name was coined only in 1954, by the art historian John I. H. Baur; Fitz Henry Lane's Maine harbours are the purest examples.
fields.Description: A strand of American landscape painting marked by glassy water, horizontal calm, and air so clear that the brushwork disappears -- the quiet opposite of its contemporaries' operatic mountain scenes.
fields.Captions: An American harbour at dusk, the brushwork invisible | John Frederick Kensett, Singing Beach, Manchester, 1862 | Kensett painting in his studio, ca. 1866 | Sanford Robinson Gifford, The Artist Sketching at Mount Desert, Maine, 1864–65, National Gallery of Art

fields.Title: Metaphysical art
fields.Artist: Giorgio de Chirico; Carlo Carrà; Giorgio Morandi
fields.Notes: Its Italian name is pittura metafisica; de Chirico and Carrà met in a Ferrara military hospital in 1917.
fields.Description: Italian paintings of deserted arcaded squares under long raking shadows, peopled by tailor's dummies, plaster casts, and stray antique statues -- a direct source for the Surrealists.
fields.Captions: Giorgio de Chirico, an arcaded square with mannequins | Giorgio de Chirico, The Disquieting Muses, 1947 version | Giorgio de Chirico, The Song of Love, 1914 | Carlo Carrà, L'ovale delle apparizioni, 1918, Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna, Rome

fields.Title: Modernism
fields.Notes: Clement Greenberg's “Modernist Painting” (1960) made flatness the criterion; Postmodernism defined itself against it.
fields.Description: The long Western turn, from about 1860, away from imitating appearances and towards the medium itself -- flatness, pure colour, abstraction -- under the principle that each art should do only what it alone can.
fields.Captions: Édouard Manet, Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe, 1863 | Paul Cézanne, Mont Sainte-Victoire, 1902–1904 | Pablo Picasso, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, 1907 | Piet Mondrian, Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow, 1930

fields.Title: Naive art
fields.Artist: Henri Rousseau; Grandma Moses; Niko Pirosmani; Séraphine Louis
fields.Notes: Henri Rousseau, a Paris toll collector, was the hero of the type for Picasso's circle, which threw him a banquet in 1908; the French term is art naïf.
fields.Description: Pictures by self-taught painters who never learned academic perspective or modelling, admired by trained artists for their flat, frontal, meticulous strangeness.
fields.Captions: Henri Rousseau, a jungle painted by a self-taught artist | Henri Rousseau, The Repast of the Lion, c. 1907, Metropolitan Museum of Art | Alfred Wallis, Noah's Ark, before 1942 | Niko Pirosmani, Deer, 1901

fields.Title: Nazarene movement
fields.Artist: Friedrich Overbeck; Franz Pforr; Peter von Cornelius; Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld
fields.Notes: They were nicknamed for their long hair and biblical dress; their example lay directly behind the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.
fields.Description: German Romantic painters who quit the Vienna academy in 1809, lived monastically in a disused Roman monastery, and set out to recover the honesty of late medieval and early Renaissance religious art.
fields.Captions: A German Romantic biblical scene in the early Italian manner | Joseph von Führich, Jacob Encountering Rachel (1836), Österreichische Galerie Belvedere | Joseph Anton Koch, Detail of the Dante-Cycle in the Casino Massimo

fields.Title: Newlyn School
fields.Artist: Stanhope Forbes; Walter Langley; Frank Bramley; Elizabeth Forbes
fields.Notes: Stanhope Forbes's A Fish Sale on a Cornish Beach (1885) made its reputation; the Lamorna group and the St Ives painters grew out of it.
fields.Description: A fishing-village colony of British painters who worked out of doors in the square-brush manner learned in Brittany, painting the harbour's labour and its bereavements.
fields.Captions: Stanhope Forbes, A Fish Sale on a Cornish Beach, 1885 | Stanhope Forbes, The Munitions Girls, 1918 | Frank Bramley, A Hopeless Dawn, 1888 | Walter Langley, Between the Tides, 1901

fields.Title: Orientalism
fields.Artist: Jean-Léon Gérôme; Eugène Delacroix; John Frederick Lewis; Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
fields.Notes: Edward Said's 1978 book gave the word its critical edge; Delacroix's 1832 Moroccan journey and Gérôme's staged harems are the standard cases.
fields.Description: European pictures of North Africa and the Near East -- bazaars, harems, slave markets, snake charmers -- painted with documentary polish for a public that mostly wanted the exotic.
fields.Captions: A European painting of a Near Eastern reception | Unknown Venetian artist, The Reception of the Ambassadors in Damascus, 1511, Louvre | Eugène Delacroix, The Women of Algiers, 1834, Louvre | Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Snake Charmer, c. 1879, Clark Art Institute

fields.Title: Ottonian Renaissance
fields.Notes: Bishop Bernward's bronze doors and column at Hildesheim (c. 1015) and the Gospels of Otto III are its masterpieces.
fields.Description: The revival of learning, manuscript illumination, and large-scale bronze casting under three German emperors of the same name, looking back to Carolingian and Byzantine models.
fields.Captions: The Lothair Cross, c. 1000 | The Essen cross with large enamels with gems and large senkschmelz enamels, c. 1000 | “Roma”, “Gallia”, “Germania”, and “Sclavinia” pay homage to Otto III, from the Munich Gospels of Otto III, one of the “Liuthar group” | Codex Egberti, Resurrection of Lazarus, “Ruodprecht group”

fields.Title: Peredvizhniki
fields.Artist: Ilya Repin; Ivan Kramskoi; Vasily Surikov; Isaac Levitan
fields.Notes: Known in English as the Wanderers or Itinerants; Repin's Barge Haulers on the Volga (1873) is the best-known canvas, and Pavel Tretyakov bought their work wholesale.
fields.Description: Russian realists who resigned from the St Petersburg academy and took their exhibitions round the provinces by train, painting serfdom, exile, poverty, and their own landscape.
fields.Captions: Ivan Shishkin, Morning in a Pine Forest, 1889 | Ilya Repin, Barge Haulers on the Volga, 1870–73 | Ivan Shishkin and Konstantin Savitsky, Morning in a Pine Forest, 1889 | The Artel of Artists (1863–1864), with Ivan Kramskoi
