fields.Title: Performance art
fields.Artist: Marina Abramović; Joseph Beuys; Yoko Ono; Chris Burden
fields.Notes: Beuys spent three days in a room with a coyote for I Like America and America Likes Me (1974); Abramović sat facing visitors for 736 hours at the MoMA in 2010.
fields.Description: Work whose medium is a live action carried out by the artist in front of an audience, surviving afterwards only as photographs, film, and description.
fields.Captions: A poster for a Joseph Beuys action | Helen Moller dancing, photographed by Arnold Genthe, early 20th century | Revived Cabaret Voltaire on the Spiegelgasse street 1 in Zürich, 2011

fields.Title: Pont-Aven School
fields.Artist: Paul Gauguin; Émile Bernard; Paul Sérusier; Charles Filiger
fields.Notes: Paul Sérusier painted The Talisman there in 1888 under Gauguin's instruction and carried it back to Paris, where it founded the Nabis.
fields.Description: The circle that gathered round Gauguin in a Breton village, painting flat unshaded colour inside heavy outlines and treating peasant piety as something primitive and visionary.
fields.Captions: A Breton landscape in flat unshaded colour | Paul Gauguin, Watermill in Pont-Aven, 1894, Musée d'Orsay | Robert Wylie, La Sorcière bretonne, 1872 | Randolph Caldecott, Pont-Aven, 1881

fields.Title: Primitivism
fields.Artist: Paul Gauguin; Pablo Picasso; André Derain; Emil Nolde
fields.Notes: Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) after visiting the Trocadéro ethnographic museum; MoMA's 1984 exhibition on the subject was widely attacked for its framing.
fields.Description: The Western appetite for the art of Africa, Oceania, and pre-industrial Europe as a source of raw vitality -- a borrowing that reshaped modern form while flattening the cultures it took from.
fields.Captions: Paul Gauguin, I Raro te Oviri, 1891 | Henri Rousseau, In a Tropical Forest: Combat of a Tiger and a Buffalo, 1908–09 | Pablo Picasso, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, 1907 | Paul Gauguin, Spirit of the Dead Watching, 1892

fields.Title: Purism
fields.Notes: Launched by the 1918 manifesto Après le cubisme; its journal L'Esprit Nouveau carried Le Corbusier's architectural essays.
fields.Description: A postwar French reaction against decorative Cubism, calling for machine-like clarity and painting bottles, glasses, and guitars as smooth, precisely drawn standard objects.
fields.Captions: A still life of standard objects in machine-like clarity | Amédée Ozenfant, Nature morte, 1920–21, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art | Le Corbusier (Charles-Édouard Jeanneret), 1920, Nature morte (Still Life), oil on canvas, 80.9 cm × 99.7 cm (31.9 in × 39.3 in), Museum of Modern Art, New York | Le Corbusier, 1922, Nature morte verticale (Vertical Still Life), oil on canvas, 146.3 cm × 89.3 cm (57.6 by 35.2 inches), Kunstmuseum Basel

fields.Title: Rayonism
fields.Notes: Larionov's 1913 manifesto claimed it as the first truly Russian abstraction; the pair left for Paris in 1915 to design for Diaghilev.
fields.Description: A brief Russian abstraction built from crossing slanted shafts of colour, meant to depict not objects but the light reflected off them where the beams intersect.
fields.Captions: Mikhail Larionov, crossing shafts of colour | Mikhail Larionov, Red Rayonism, 1913 | Goncharova and other artists at a Donkey's Tail exhibition, 1912 | Natalia Goncharova, Rayonist Lilies, 1913

fields.Title: Renaissance
fields.Notes: Vasari's Lives (1550) invented the story of rebirth and decline; its Italian phases run Early (Masaccio, Donatello), High (Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo), and Mannerist.
fields.Description: The European recovery of classical learning and classical art between the 14th and 16th centuries, which restored linear perspective, anatomy, and the antique nude and turned the artist from a craftsman into a learned man.
fields.Captions: Piero della Francesca, The Baptism of Christ, 1450s, National Gallery, London | Masaccio, Holy Trinity, c. 1427, Santa Maria Novella, Florence | Raphael, The School of Athens, 1509–1511, Vatican | Titian, Sacred and Profane Love, c. 1514, Galleria Borghese, Rome

fields.Title: Romanesque
fields.Notes: Its sculpture clusters along the pilgrimage routes -- Gislebertus's Last Judgment at Autun, the tympanum at Vézelay, the cloister at Moissac.
fields.Description: The art of Western Europe before the pointed arch: round-arched churches with heavy walls and small windows, and sculpture of stretched, agitated figures squeezed into tympana and capitals.
fields.Captions: The painted vaults of the Pantheon of the Kings, San Isidoro, León, 12th century | Master of Pedret, The Virgin and Child in Majesty, apse fresco from Tredòs, Catalonia, c. 1100

fields.Title: Street art
fields.Artist: Banksy; Shepard Fairey; JR; Blek le Rat
fields.Notes: Blek le Rat's Paris stencils of the early 1980s came first, and Banksy has acknowledged the debt; JR pastes giant photographic portraits onto buildings.
fields.Description: Post-graffiti work made for public walls with stencils, paste-ups, stickers, and murals, aimed at passers-by rather than at other writers, and often satirical.
fields.Captions: The East Side Gallery on the Berlin Wall | Street art by Kevin Larmee, SoHo, New York City (1985) | The 2010 recreation of Keith Haring's original 1982 mural; New York City's Bowery Mural wall at Houston Street and the Bowery | Guerrilla art, a humanist mural by Fasim in Alcoi, 2018, Valencia, Spain

fields.Title: Synthetic Cubism
fields.Artist: Pablo Picasso; Georges Braque; Juan Gris
fields.Notes: It begins with Picasso's Still Life with Chair Caning (1912), the first collage, and Braque's papiers collés of the same year.
fields.Description: The second phase of its movement, which built pictures up instead of taking them apart: flat planes of bright colour, stencilled letters, wallpaper, oilcloth, and pasted newsprint.
fields.Captions: Juan Gris, Still Life with Checked Tablecloth, 1915 | Juan Gris, Woman with a Mandolin, after Corot, 1916

fields.Title: Synthetism
fields.Artist: Paul Gauguin; Émile Bernard; Paul Sérusier
fields.Notes: Shown at the Café Volpini in 1889 by the “Groupe Impressionniste et Synthétiste”; closely bound up with Cloisonnism.
fields.Description: Gauguin's principle that a picture should fuse the look of the subject, the feeling it provoked, and the demands of flat decorative design, with colour and line chosen for their own sake rather than for accuracy.
fields.Captions: A Breton landscape in flat decorative colour | Paul Sérusier, The Talisman, 1888 | Paul Sérusier, The Talisman, 1888, Musée d'Orsay | Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Portrait of Émile Bernard, 1886

fields.Title: Tonalism
fields.Artist: George Inness; James McNeill Whistler; Dwight William Tryon
fields.Notes: Owes much to the Barbizon painters and to Whistler's Nocturnes; George Inness's late work is the central body of it.
fields.Description: An American landscape manner of soft, hazy, atmospheric views kept within a narrow range of one colour -- dusk, fog, and moonlight painted as a mood rather than a place.
fields.Captions: James McNeill Whistler, a Nocturne | George Inness, In the Berkshires, 1850 | George Inness, The Lackawanna Valley, c. 1856, National Gallery of Art | George Inness, Lake Albano, 1869, Phillips Collection

fields.Title: Umbrian School
fields.Notes: Perugino's Delivery of the Keys in the Sistine Chapel is the model composition, and Raphael's early Marriage of the Virgin follows it closely.
fields.Description: Central Italian painters of sweet-faced, gently posed figures placed in wide, airy, deeply receding landscapes, from the hill region that produced Raphael's teacher.
fields.Captions: Perugino, Delivery of the Keys, Sistine Chapel | Città della Pieve | Pietro Perugino, The Delivery of the Keys, 1481–82, Sistine Chapel | God the Father and angels by Pietro Perugino on the ceiling of Stanza dell'Incendio del Borgo

fields.Title: Utagawa School
fields.Notes: Founded by Toyoharu; pupils took the school's name as their own, so Hiroshige, Kuniyoshi, and Kunisada all signed with it.
fields.Description: The largest workshop lineage in Japanese woodblock printmaking, which dominated the 19th-century market for actor portraits, warrior prints, and landscape series.
fields.Captions: A Japanese woodblock bird-and-flower print | Hiroshige, Mandarin Ducks | Hiroshige, Wind-Blown Grass across the Moon, c. 1832 | Utagawa Toyohiro, Hiroshige's teacher, Returning Sails at Tsukuda, from Eight Views of Edo, 1802–29

fields.Title: Venetian School
fields.Artist: Giovanni Bellini; Titian; Tintoretto; Paolo Veronese
fields.Notes: Its colorito was set against Florentine disegno in a long critical argument; Titian's late broken handling led directly to Rubens and Velázquez.
fields.Description: The Italian tradition that put colour and light before drawn outline, worked in oil on canvas because damp walls ruined fresco, and loosened its brushstroke steadily over three centuries.
fields.Captions: Titian, colour and light before drawn outline | Giovanni Bellini, San Zaccaria Altarpiece, 1505, San Zaccaria, Venice | Paolo Veneziano, polyptych with the Coronation of the Virgin, c. 1350 | Carlo Crivelli, The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius, 1486

fields.Title: Video art
fields.Artist: Nam June Paik; Bill Viola; Bruce Nauman; Joan Jonas
fields.Notes: Nam June Paik is usually credited with starting it in 1965, the year the Sony Portapak reached consumers; his TV Buddha watches itself on a closed circuit.
fields.Description: Work made with the portable recording camera and the monitor from the mid-1960s on, whether as sculpture built from stacked screens or as slow projected sequences filling a darkened room.
fields.Captions: Nam June Paik, TV Cello, 1966 | Nam June Paik, Pre-Bell-Man, 1989 | A Sony AV-3400 Portapak | A still from Joan Jonas's 1972 video

fields.Title: Vorticism
fields.Artist: Wyndham Lewis; Henri Gaudier-Brzeska; David Bomberg; Edward Wadsworth
fields.Notes: Ezra Pound named it; its journal BLAST ran two issues in 1914–15, and Gaudier-Brzeska's death at the front in 1915 broke the group.
fields.Description: A short-lived British answer to Cubism and Futurism, built from hard diagonal machine forms driving in towards a still centre, and killed off by the First World War.
fields.Captions: A British machine-age composition, c. 1915 | Edward Wadsworth, Vorticist Study, 1914, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid | Jacob Epstein's Rock Drill in his studio, c. 1913 | Wyndham Lewis, The Dancers, 1912

fields.Title: Young British Artists
fields.Artist: Damien Hirst; Tracey Emin; Sarah Lucas; Chris Ofili
fields.Notes: Hirst organized the 1988 warehouse show Freeze; the 1997 Royal Academy exhibition Sensation drew protests in London and New York.
fields.Description: The London generation that came out of Goldsmiths from 1988, made shock and publicity part of the work itself, and was bought almost wholesale by the advertising magnate Charles Saatchi.
fields.Captions: Damien Hirst, The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living, 1991 | Tracey Emin, My Bed, 1998 | Chris Ofili, The Holy Virgin Mary, 1996

fields.Title: Aestheticism
fields.Artist: James McNeill Whistler; Dante Gabriel Rossetti; Aubrey Beardsley; Albert Moore
fields.Notes: Ruskin's attack on Whistler's Nocturne in Black and Gold as “flinging a pot of paint in the public's face” brought the 1878 libel trial that Whistler won for a farthing.
fields.Description: The late Victorian doctrine that a picture owes nothing to story or morality and exists only for its own beauty -- “art for art's sake”.
fields.Captions: Whistler's Peacock Room | Albert Joseph Moore, Canaries, c. 1875–80 | Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Lady Lilith

fields.Title: Art brut
fields.Artist: Adolf Wölfli; Aloïse Corbaz; Augustin Lesage; Madge Gill
fields.Notes: Dubuffet coined the term in 1945 and left his collection to Lausanne; the English “outsider art” is Roger Cardinal's 1972 rendering of it.
fields.Description: Work made entirely outside any culture of art -- by psychiatric patients, prisoners, and visionaries -- and collected by Jean Dubuffet as the only kind uncontaminated by training and fashion.
fields.Captions: A drawing by a self-taught psychiatric patient | Adolf Wölfli, Irren-Anstalt Band-Hain, 1910 | Anna Zemánková, Untitled, 1960s | Niko Pirosmani, Deer, 1901

fields.Title: Byzantine art
fields.Notes: Hagia Sophia, the mosaics of San Vitale at Ravenna and the icons of Saint Catherine's at Sinai are its landmarks; the Iconoclast controversy destroyed most of the earlier work.
fields.Description: The art of the Eastern Roman Empire: gold-ground mosaics and panel paintings of frontal, weightless, elongated saints, held to a fixed iconography for a thousand years.
fields.Captions: The Deësis mosaic, Hagia Sophia | The Arab Saint Arethas depicted in traditional Byzantine style (10th century) | Frescoes at Nerezi near Skopje (1164), anticipating Giotto | Interior of the Rotunda of St. George, Thessaloniki, with remnants of the mosaics

fields.Title: Genre painting
fields.Artist: Jan Steen; Pieter de Hooch; Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin; Pieter Bruegel the Elder
fields.Notes: A Dutch speciality of the 17th century; the French academy ranked it third of five, above landscape and still life.
fields.Description: Pictures of ordinary people doing ordinary things -- taverns, kitchens, card games, courtships -- placed below scripture, myth, and portraiture in the academic ranking of subjects.
fields.Captions: Nicolaes Maes, The Idle Servant, 1655 | Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Peasant Dance, c. 1567

fields.Title: Gesamtkunstwerk
fields.Notes: Set out in Wagner's essays of 1849 and built for at Bayreuth; the word means “total work of art”.
fields.Description: Wagner's ideal of a single work in which music, poetry, staging, design, and dance are fused so completely that no one art dominates -- later taken up by Art Nouveau designers and by the Bauhaus.
fields.Captions: An Art Nouveau interior designed down to the fittings | Stairway of the Hôtel Tassel, an early example of Gesamtkunstwerk | A page of the score of Richard Wagner's Die Walküre | Stoclet Palace, 1905–1911

fields.Title: Grand Manner
fields.Artist: Joshua Reynolds; Nicolas Poussin; Benjamin West; Pompeo Batoni
fields.Notes: Reynolds set it out in his Discourses at the Royal Academy and posed his sitters as classical deities and heroes.
fields.Description: The elevated style prescribed for the highest subjects, and for portraits that borrow its poses: idealized figures, classical drapery, and noble gesture, generalized away from particular detail.
fields.Captions: Joshua Reynolds, Mrs Siddons as the Tragic Muse, 1784 | A portrait of Benjamin West, 1770, National Portrait Gallery, Washington | Pompeo Batoni, John Talbot, later 1st Earl Talbot, 1773, Getty Museum | Raphael, The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple, 1512, Vatican

fields.Title: Happening
fields.Artist: Allan Kaprow; Jim Dine; Claes Oldenburg; Red Grooms
fields.Notes: Allan Kaprow's 18 Happenings in 6 Parts (1959) at the Reuben Gallery named the form, which grew out of John Cage's classes at the New School.
fields.Description: A loosely scripted event staged in a gallery or a loft, which draws the audience into the action, is not repeated, and leaves nothing behind to sell.
fields.Captions: An assemblage environment of the early 1960s | Survival Research Laboratories performance in Chinatown, Los Angeles, January 2006 | Jean-Jacques Lebel–at Exhibition Beat Generation, November 2013 | Beuys Felt TV performance by Lothar Wolleh in 1971

fields.Title: History painting
fields.Artist: Jacques-Louis David; Nicolas Poussin; Peter Paul Rubens; Benjamin West
fields.Notes: Benjamin West's The Death of General Wolfe (1770) broke the convention by dressing a modern subject in modern clothes.
fields.Description: The kind of picture the academies ranked highest: many figures in significant action, drawn from scripture, myth or the classical past, demanding learning as well as skill.
fields.Captions: Titian, Diana and Actaeon, 1556–59 | Rembrandt, Judas Returning the Thirty Pieces of Silver, 1629 | Jacques-Louis David, Oath of the Horatii, 1784

fields.Title: Humanism
fields.Notes: Petrarch is counted its founder; Pico della Mirandola's Oration on the Dignity of Man (1486) is its manifesto, and Alberti and Leonardo are its artist-scholars.
fields.Description: The Renaissance program of study built on recovered classical texts, which put man at the centre of the picture -- hence anatomy, portraiture, the nude, and buildings proportioned to the body.
fields.Captions: Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man, c. 1490 | Giorgio Vasari, Six Tuscan Poets, 1544

fields.Title: International Gothic
fields.Artist: Gentile da Fabriano; Limbourg brothers; Pisanello; Simone Martini
fields.Notes: The Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry and Gentile da Fabriano's Adoration of the Magi (1423) are its high points.
fields.Description: A courtly manner that travelled between Paris, Prague, Milan, and Burgundy around 1400: elegant, elongated figures, gold grounds, rich costume, and minutely observed birds, animals, and flowers.
fields.Captions: A courtly miniature of about 1400 | Colart de Laon, The Agony in the Garden with the Donor Louis I, Duke of Orléans, c. 1405–08, Prado | Simone Martini, The Annunciation (detail), 1333, Uffizi | Lorenzo Monaco, The Flight into Egypt, predella panel, c. 1405

fields.Title: Kinetic art
fields.Artist: Alexander Calder; Jean Tinguely; Naum Gabo; Len Lye
fields.Notes: Naum Gabo's motorized Standing Wave (1920) is an early instance; Duchamp named Calder's hanging mobiles, and Tinguely's Homage to New York destroyed itself in MoMA's garden in 1960.
fields.Description: Sculpture that actually moves, whether on air currents, under a motor, or as the viewer's own position shifts around it.
fields.Captions: A sculpture built to move | Naum Gabo, Kinetic Construction (Standing Wave), 1919–20 | Jean Tinguely, Eos, 1965 | George Rickey, Four Squares in Square Arrangement, 1969, Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin

fields.Title: Naturalism
fields.Artist: Jules Bastien-Lepage; Gustave Courbet; Thomas Eakins; Jean-François Millet
fields.Notes: Often used interchangeably with Realism, though critics reserve this word for close observation and the other for a social argument; Zola's literary use shaped the term.
fields.Description: Painting that sets down what is actually in front of the artist, unflattering detail included, without arranging it towards an ideal or a moral.
fields.Captions: A landscape set down as observed | Eilif Peterssen, Summer Night, 1886 | Francisco Goya, Charles IV of Spain and His Family, 1800–01 | Henri Biva, Matin à Villeneuve, c. 1905–06

fields.Title: New Objectivity
fields.Artist: Otto Dix; George Grosz; Max Beckmann; Christian Schad
fields.Notes: Its German name is Neue Sachlichkeit, coined for a 1925 exhibition in Mannheim; Dix's War triptych and Grosz's caricatures are central to it.
fields.Description: The hard, cold, satirical realism of Weimar Germany, which turned from Expressionist feeling to painting war cripples, profiteers, and prostitutes in pitiless detail.
fields.Captions: George Grosz, Pillars of Society, 1926 | Alexander Kanoldt, Still Life with Jugs and Red Tea Caddy, 1922 | Hans Mertens, Card Players, 1929 | Panorama of the IG Farben Building from the south. The curved shape of the building's façade reduces the impact of its scale.

fields.Title: Kitsch
fields.Notes: The word came out of the Munich art market of the 1860s–70s; Clement Greenberg's “Avant-Garde and Kitsch” (1939) set the opposition, and Jeff Koons later embraced the charge.
fields.Description: Cheap, sentimental, mass-produced prettiness, used since the 1930s as the negative against which serious modern art defines itself.
fields.Captions: Dogs Playing Poker, C. M. Coolidge | Cassius Marcellus Coolidge, A Friend in Need, from the Dogs Playing Poker series, 1903 | Jeff Koons, Puppy | A mass-produced teapot and milk jug set, themed after a rural cottage

fields.Title: Avant-garde
fields.Notes: Henri de Saint-Simon applied the military figure to artists in 1825; Clement Greenberg opposed it to kitsch in 1939, and Peter Bürger's Theory of the Avant-Garde (1974) distinguished it from Modernism.
fields.Description: The metaphor, borrowed from soldiering, for the small group of artists working out ahead of public taste, whose innovations the rest of the culture catches up with later.
fields.Captions: Lyubov Popova, Composition, 1917 | The Overthrow of the Autocracy, a Soviet avant-garde painting, c. 1917 | Walter Benjamin, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” (1935)

fields.Title: Eileen Agar
fields.Notes: A Tate retrospective in 2021 brought her back into view; she photographed the Surrealist circle as well as painting it.
fields.Description: Argentine-born British Surrealist who made assemblages out of shells, driftwood, and other found natural objects, and was the only British woman in the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London.
fields.Captions: Eileen Agar
fields.Works: Angel of Anarchy; Ceremonial Hat for Eating Bouillabaisse; The Autobiography of an Embryo

fields.Title: Craigie Aitchison
fields.Notes: Trained at the Slade and sent to Italy on a scholarship; the Isle of Arran and Italian hill towns are his other standing subjects.
fields.Description: Scottish painter of luminous, near-empty pictures built from flat blocks of vivid colour, who returned again and again to the Crucifixion and habitually put his Bedlington terriers into it.
fields.Captions: Craigie Aitchison
fields.Works: Crucifixion (many versions, one behind the altar in Liverpool Cathedral's chapter house); Holy Island; portraits of Naaotwa Swayne

fields.Title: Michael Andrews
fields.Notes: His output was small and unhurried; the balloon paintings of the 1970s look down on the land from above, and his last years went on Ayers Rock and the Thames.
fields.Description: English figurative painter loosely of the School of London, who worked slowly on large group scenes -- a Soho drinking club, a party, swimmers -- and turned later to aerial landscapes and hot-air balloons.
fields.Captions: Michael Andrews
fields.Works: The Colony Room I; Melanie and Me Swimming; the Lights series; The Cathedral, North East Face (Uluru)

fields.Title: Antonello da Messina
fields.Notes: Vasari claimed he learned oil painting from Jan van Eyck himself, which is chronologically impossible; his stay in Venice in 1475-76 changed Venetian painting.
fields.Description: Sicilian Early Renaissance painter credited with carrying the Netherlandish oil technique into Italy, whose small, intensely observed half-length portraits look straight out at the viewer.
fields.Captions: Portrait of a Man, c. 1475, generally taken to be a self-portrait
fields.Works: Saint Jerome in His Study; Virgin Annunciate; Portrait of a Man (Il Condottiero); San Cassiano Altarpiece

fields.Title: Terry Atkinson
fields.Notes: Art & Language began in Coventry in 1968 and is the standard English-language reference point for Conceptual art.
fields.Description: English conceptual artist, a founder of the Art & Language group, which replaced the art object with text, theory, and argument; he left in the mid-1970s for drawings about war, class, and labour.
fields.Works: Map to Not Indicate (1967, with Michael Baldwin); the Art-Language journal, from 1969; the Ruins of Empire drawings

fields.Title: Hendrick Avercamp
fields.Notes: Nicknamed de Stomme van Kampen, “the mute of Kampen”; the high vantage point and tiny incidental figures descend from Bruegel.
fields.Description: Deaf and mute Dutch Golden Age painter who specialized in winter: crowded panoramas of frozen canals full of skaters, sledges, and golfers drawn from every social class.
fields.Captions: Hendrick Avercamp
fields.Works: Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters; Winter Scene on a Canal; A Scene on the Ice near a Town

fields.Title: Gillian Ayres
fields.Notes: The 1957 school mural was painted with the panels flat on the floor in direct response to Pollock; Turner Prize nominee in 1989.
fields.Description: English abstract painter of huge, thickly loaded canvases in clashing hot colour, who moved from 1950s gestural staining to late paintings full of circles, loops, and organic shapes.
fields.Captions: Gillian Ayres
fields.Works: Distillation; Antony and Cleopatra; the South Hampstead High School mural; the Old Marylebone Town Hall ceiling

fields.Title: Balthus
fields.Notes: Rilke, his mother's lover, published his drawing series Mitsou when he was thirteen; he ran the French Academy in Rome for sixteen years and invented a noble title for himself.
fields.Description: Polish-French painter of airless, deliberately archaic interiors in which adolescent girls doze or stretch in poses borrowed from Piero della Francesca -- pictures still argued over for their eroticism.
fields.Captions: Balthus at Rossinière, 2000
fields.Works: Thérèse Dreaming; The Guitar Lesson; The Street; The Mountain

fields.Title: Jacopo Bassano
fields.Notes: Four of his sons carried on the family workshop; the night scenes and the animal detail fed directly into later Baroque genre painting.
fields.Description: Venetian-school painter who spent his life in the small Veneto town he took his surname from, treating biblical stories as farmyard scenes full of peasants, sheep, dogs, and copper pots.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait
fields.Works: The Adoration of the Shepherds; The Last Supper; Jacob's Journey; The Way to Calvary

fields.Title: Vanessa Bell
fields.Notes: Sister of Virginia Woolf; she co-founded the Omega Workshops with Roger Fry in 1913, and Charleston Farmhouse, painted throughout with Duncan Grant, is now a museum.
fields.Description: English painter and designer of the Bloomsbury circle, whose flattened, boldly coloured domestic scenes and still lifes follow Cézanne and Matisse; she decorated a Sussex farmhouse from floor to ceiling.
fields.Captions: Vanessa Bell
fields.Works: Studland Beach; A Conversation; Virginia Woolf in a Deckchair; the Charleston interiors

fields.Title: John Bellany
fields.Notes: A liver transplant in 1988 nearly killed him and changed the work: the late paintings are far more brightly coloured, and he drew himself in the hospital bed throughout.
fields.Description: Scottish painter of harsh, symbol-laden figure pictures drawn from the fishing village he grew up in -- gutted fish, oilskins, harbour walls -- darkened further after a visit to Buchenwald.
fields.Captions: John Bellany, Allegory, 1964
fields.Works: Allegory; Kinlochbervie; Homage to John Knox; the Addenbrooke's hospital self-portraits

fields.Title: Peter Blake
fields.Notes: He later founded the Brotherhood of Ruralists; his other sleeves include The Who's Face Dances and Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas?
fields.Description: English Pop artist who built collages out of badges, comics, wrestlers, and fairground signs, and designed one of the most reproduced record sleeves ever made.
fields.Captions: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band sleeve, 1967
fields.Works: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band sleeve, 1967, with Jann Haworth; On the Balcony; Self-Portrait with Badges; The Meeting, or Have a Nice Day, Mr Hockney

fields.Title: Christian Boltanski
fields.Notes: Almost nothing in the photographs is what it claims to be; he called the work an archive of a childhood he largely invented, and filled the Grand Palais with fifty tonnes of clothing in 2010.
fields.Description: French installation artist who built rooms out of grainy enlarged snapshots, rusted biscuit tins, piles of second-hand clothes, and bare bulbs, staging memory and the anonymous dead.
fields.Captions: Christian Boltanski
fields.Works: Réserve: Les Suisses morts; Personnes; The Missing House; Monument

fields.Title: Eugène Boudin
fields.Notes: Corot called him the “king of the skies”; he exhibited in the first Impressionist show of 1874 although he belonged to the generation before it.
fields.Description: French painter of Normandy beaches and harbours whose small, quick studies of crowded sands under enormous skies bridged academic landscape and Impressionism; he took the young Monet outdoors to paint.
fields.Captions: Eugène Boudin
fields.Works: The Beach at Trouville; Bathers on the Beach at Trouville; the Honfleur and Deauville harbour scenes; hundreds of cloud studies

fields.Title: Dieric Bouts
fields.Notes: The Leuven altarpiece came with a theologians' contract specifying its subjects; The Entombment is a rare survival in glue-size tempera on linen.
fields.Description: Early Netherlandish painter working in Leuven, whose stiff, elongated figures stand in deep, carefully receding landscapes; his Last Supper altarpiece is among the first pictures built on a single vanishing point.
fields.Captions: Engraved portrait of Dieric Bouts | Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament, 1464–67
fields.Works: Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament (The Last Supper); The Justice of Emperor Otto III; The Entombment; Virgin and Child

fields.Title: Sonia Boyce
fields.Notes: Feeling Her Way won the Golden Lion for best national pavilion in 2022; she is Professor of Black Art and Design at the University of the Arts London.
fields.Description: British artist of the 1980s Black Arts Movement who moved from large pastel self-portraits about race and family into collaborative work with singers and performers; the first Black woman to represent Britain in Venice.
fields.Works: Feeling Her Way (Venice, 2022); Missionary Position II; She Ain't Holding Them Up, She's Holding On; Devotional Collection

fields.Title: Arthur Boyd
fields.Notes: He gave his Shoalhaven property, Bundanon, and his collection to Australia; he represented the country at the 1958 Venice Biennale.
fields.Description: Australian painter from a long artistic dynasty, who set biblical and mythological stories in the bush and painted a mixed-race bride and her groom as a parable of dispossession.
fields.Captions: Arthur Boyd
fields.Works: Love, Marriage and Death of a Half-caste (the Bride series); The Expulsion; the Shoalhaven River paintings; the Nebuchadnezzar series

fields.Title: John Bratby
fields.Notes: He painted the pictures attributed to Gulley Jimson in the 1958 film of The Horse's Mouth, and wrote novels as well.
fields.Description: English painter who founded the Kitchen Sink school: cluttered bedsits, cornflake packets, unmade beds, and dustbins, laid on in thick, angry paint against both abstraction and prettiness.
fields.Works: Still Life with Chip Frier; Jean and Still Life in Front of a Window; Table Top; the canvases painted for the film The Horse's Mouth

fields.Title: Jan Brueghel the Elder
fields.Notes: Nicknamed “Velvet” for his textures; brother of Pieter Brueghel the Younger and ancestor of a whole dynasty of painters.
fields.Description: Flemish painter, the younger son of a famous peasant-painting father, known for jewel-like flower pieces, paradise landscapes, and allegories of the senses, often with Rubens supplying the figures.
fields.Captions: Jan Brueghel the Elder with his family, painted by Peter Paul Rubens, c. 1613
fields.Works: Flowers in a Wooden Vessel; The Garden of Eden with the Fall of Man (with Rubens); The Allegory of Sight; Battle of Issus

fields.Title: Edward Burne-Jones
fields.Notes: He met William Morris at Oxford and was taught by Rossetti; the 1877 Grosvenor Gallery exhibition made his reputation overnight.
fields.Description: English painter and designer of the second Pre-Raphaelite generation, whose pale, elongated knights and sleeping princesses come out of Malory, Chaucer, and Greek myth; he designed stained glass for Morris & Co. for forty years.
fields.Captions: Edward Burne-Jones, photographed by Frederick Hollyer, about 1882
fields.Works: King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid; The Golden Stairs; The Briar Rose series; Love Among the Ruins; the Kelmscott Chaucer illustrations

fields.Title: Edward Burra
fields.Notes: Crippled by arthritis and anaemia from childhood, he painted sitting at a table, which is part of why he used watercolour rather than oil.
fields.Description: English painter who worked almost entirely in watercolour, on a scale usually reserved for oils, on nightclubs, dockside bars, and Harlem street life in the 1930s, and on bleak English landscapes after the war.
fields.Captions: Edward Burra
fields.Works: The Snack Bar; Harlem; Izzy Orts; Soldiers at Rye

fields.Title: Miriam Cahn
fields.Notes: She began by drawing at night in black chalk directly onto walls and bridges in Basel; a 2023 Paris retrospective drew protests and a legal challenge over one painting.
fields.Description: Swiss painter of raw, staring figures in acid colour -- bodies under threat, migrants, victims of war -- made fast and left unpolished, out of the feminist art of the 1970s.
fields.Captions: Miriam Cahn, o.T. (Untitled), 2012
fields.Works: o.T. (Untitled) figure paintings; Strategische Orte; Das Klassische Lieben

fields.Title: Anthony Caro
fields.Notes: He worked as Henry Moore's assistant, then a 1959 trip to America and meeting David Smith changed everything; he taught a generation at St Martin's.
fields.Description: English sculptor who took the plinth away: welded assemblages of I-beams, girders, and sheet steel, painted a single flat colour, standing directly on the floor with the viewer.
fields.Captions: Anthony Caro
fields.Works: Early One Morning; Midday; Month of May; Sculpture Two

fields.Title: Patrick Caulfield
fields.Notes: He disliked being called a Pop artist; the inset photorealistic panels -- an alpine travel poster, a lobster -- are the signature device.
fields.Description: English painter of restaurant interiors, pub lamps, and pottery, drawn in flat black outline on saturated single-colour grounds, with one hyper-realistic passage dropped in to disturb the flatness.
fields.Captions: Patrick Caulfield, After Lunch, 1975
fields.Works: After Lunch; Pottery; Dining Recess; Still Life: Autumn Fashion

fields.Title: Helen Chadwick
fields.Notes: Piss Flowers are bronze casts of the cavities she and her partner urinated into the snow; she died suddenly at 42.
fields.Description: English sculptor and photographer who used chocolate, meat, lambs' tongues, flowers, and rotting vegetables to unsettle ideas of the body; one of the first women shortlisted for the Turner Prize.
fields.Captions: Helen Chadwick | Piss Flowers, 1991–92
fields.Works: Piss Flowers; Of Mutability (Oval Court); Cacao; Loop My Loop

fields.Title: Sandro Chia
fields.Notes: The critic Achille Bonito Oliva grouped him with Clemente, Cucchi, De Maria, and Paladino as the Transavanguardia in 1979.
fields.Description: Italian painter and sculptor of the 1980s Transavanguardia, whose muscular, swaggering figures in hot colour deliberately revived myth and heroic painting against Conceptual and Minimal art.
fields.Captions: Sandro Chia, Table of Peace, 2003, Tel Aviv Museum of Art
fields.Works: The Idleness of Sisyphus; Water Bearer; Genoa; Table of Peace

fields.Title: Eduardo Chillida
fields.Notes: He trained as an architect and kept goal for Real Sociedad until a knee injury; the open-air museum Chillida Leku near San Sebastián holds his work.
fields.Description: Basque sculptor of massive forged iron and concrete forms that grip empty space between their arms, best known for a three-pronged steel piece anchored in the rocks of a San Sebastián headland.
fields.Captions: Eduardo Chillida | The Comb of the Wind, San Sebastián, 1976
fields.Works: The Comb of the Wind (Peine del Viento); Homage to Tolerance; Elogio del Horizonte; Berlin

fields.Title: Francesco Clemente
fields.Notes: He divides the year between New York, Rome, and Madras, and has made books with Allen Ginsberg and Robert Creeley.
fields.Description: Italian painter of the Transavanguardia who works in fresco, pastel, and watercolour between New York and Madras, filling the pictures with his own head, bodily openings and Hindu, and Tantric imagery.
fields.Captions: Francesco Clemente
fields.Works: The Fourteen Stations; Conversion to Her; Name; the miniatures made with Orissa scroll painters

fields.Title: Eileen Cooper
fields.Notes: Keeper of the Royal Academy Schools from 2011 to 2017, the first woman to hold the post since the Academy was founded in 1768.
fields.Description: English painter and printmaker of bold, simplified female figures in flat colour, working on motherhood, fertility, and the body through personal and mythological narrative; the Royal Academy's first woman Keeper.
fields.Works: The Mother and Child paintings; Between the Lines; woodcut and monotype series on fertility and the body

fields.Title: Joseph Cornell
fields.Notes: He hardly ever left Queens, where he looked after his mother and disabled brother; Rose Hobart (1936) is an early found-footage film that infuriated Dalí.
fields.Description: Self-taught American maker of small glass-fronted boxes packed with cut-out birds, star charts, ballerinas, clay pipes, and marbles -- Surrealist assemblage built entirely out of junk-shop finds.
fields.Captions: Joseph Cornell, Untitled (The Hotel Eden), c. 1945
fields.Works: Untitled (Soap Bubble Set); the Medici Slot Machine boxes; the Aviary series; the film Rose Hobart

fields.Title: Juan Sánchez Cotán
fields.Notes: He gave up secular painting in 1603 to enter the Carthusian order at Granada; the produce hangs from strings to keep it from vermin, and the arrangement follows a hyperbolic curve.
fields.Description: Spanish Carthusian monk and pioneer of the bodegón: a few vegetables and fruits hung on strings or set on a stone ledge in a black window recess, arranged along a strict mathematical curve.
fields.Captions: Juan Sánchez Cotán, Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber, c. 1602
fields.Works: Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber; Still Life with Game Fowl; Still Life with Cardoon and Carrots

fields.Title: John Sell Cotman
fields.Notes: Leader of the Norwich School with John Crome; he taught drawing for years in Yarmouth and etched hundreds of plates of Norman architecture in Normandy.
fields.Description: English watercolourist of the Norwich School, who laid flat, unmodulated washes into simple, almost abstract blocks of tone -- a bridge, a ruined abbey, a plowed field -- and etched medieval architecture by the hundred.
fields.Captions: John Sell Cotman, drawn by his son Miles Edmund Cotman
fields.Works: Greta Bridge; Chirk Aqueduct; The Drop Gate; Norwich Market Place

fields.Title: John Robert Cozens
fields.Notes: Constable called him “the greatest genius that ever touched landscape”; he went insane in 1794 and was cared for by Dr Thomas Monro until his death.
fields.Description: English watercolourist of Alpine and Italian scenes in a narrow range of blues, greys, and greens, whose spacious, melancholy views were copied by the young Turner and Girtin at Dr Monro's house.
fields.Captions: John Robert Cozens, The Lake of Albano and Castel Gandolfo
fields.Works: The Lake of Albano and Castel Gandolfo; Between Chamonix and Martigny; Padua in a Storm

fields.Title: Tony Cragg
fields.Notes: Turner Prize 1988 and the British pavilion at that year's Venice Biennale; he runs the Waldfrieden sculpture park in Wuppertal.
fields.Description: British sculptor, long resident in Germany, who began by arranging coloured plastic rubbish into wall-mounted silhouettes and now makes towering twisted columns of bronze, wood, and stone that look as though they are spinning.
fields.Captions: Tony Cragg
fields.Works: Britain Seen from the North; New Stones -- Newton's Tones; Points of View; Runner

fields.Title: Carlo Crivelli
fields.Notes: He signed himself Carolus Crivellus Venetus long after leaving Venice; the cucumber and the gourd are his personal emblems and turn up in almost every picture.
fields.Description: Venetian-born painter who spent his career in the Marches, holding to gold grounds and Late Gothic ornament while using ferociously precise perspective, and hanging real-looking cucumbers and apples in front of his saints.
fields.Captions: Carlo Crivelli, The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius, 1486
fields.Works: The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius; The Demidoff Altarpiece; Madonna della Candeletta; Pietà

fields.Title: Aelbert Cuyp
fields.Notes: Collected obsessively by the 18th-century English, which is why so much of his work hangs in Britain; he married a rich widow in 1658 and largely stopped painting.
fields.Description: Dutch Golden Age landscape painter of Dordrecht, who bathed river views, cattle, and horsemen in a low golden Italianate light learned from Claude without ever leaving the Netherlands.
fields.Captions: Engraved portrait of Aelbert Cuyp | The Maas at Dordrecht, c. 1650
fields.Works: The Maas at Dordrecht; River Landscape with Horseman and Peasants; Herdsmen with Cows; A Distant View of Dordrecht

fields.Title: Richard Deacon
fields.Notes: Turner Prize 1987; one of the New British Sculpture generation with Cragg, Woodrow, and Wilding, and he represented Wales at Venice in 2007.
fields.Description: British sculptor who calls himself a fabricator: large open forms of laminated wood, riveted steel, ceramic, and linoleum, with the glue, screws, and joints deliberately left showing.
fields.Captions: Richard Deacon
fields.Works: For Those Who Have Ears #2; Two Can Play; Fold; Nose to Nose, Blind to the World

fields.Title: Joan Eardley
fields.Notes: She died of breast cancer at 42; the Catterline seascapes were painted outdoors in gales with the board weighted down against the wind.
fields.Description: British painter of two subjects only: ragged children in the Glasgow tenements of Townhead, and the sea and fields at a Kincardineshire fishing village, painted in heavy impasto with grass and newspaper pressed into the paint.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait
fields.Works: Two Children; Catterline in Winter; Salmon Net Posts; The Wave

fields.Title: Jacob Epstein
fields.Notes: The British Medical Association building's figures were later hacked off as unsafe; the Wilde tomb was censored, and its missing parts are the subject of a long-running cemetery anecdote.
fields.Description: American-born British sculptor whose rough, primitivist carvings caused scandal after scandal -- a robot figure mounted on a real rock drill, naked figures on a Strand building, a winged tomb for Oscar Wilde.
fields.Captions: Jacob Epstein | The Rock Drill, 1913–15, in the 1974 reconstruction at the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery
fields.Works: The Rock Drill; Tomb of Oscar Wilde; Day and Night (London Underground headquarters); Jacob and the Angel; Madonna and Child, Cavendish Square

fields.Title: Lyonel Feininger
fields.Notes: His comic strips The Kin-der-Kids and Wee Willie Winkie's World ran in the Chicago Tribune in 1906; the Nazis put him in the Degenerate Art show and he left for New York in 1937.
fields.Description: German-American painter who began as a newspaper cartoonist and ended making cathedrals, ships, and village churches out of transparent, overlapping prismatic planes; the Bauhaus's first appointed master.
fields.Captions: Lyonel Feininger
fields.Works: Cathedral (the woodcut on the 1919 Bauhaus manifesto); the Gelmeroda series; Bird Cloud; The Steamer Odin II

fields.Title: Elisabeth Frink
fields.Notes: One of the “Geometry of Fear” sculptors of the 1950s; the Goggle Heads came out of photographs of the Moroccan general Mohamed Oufkir.
fields.Description: English sculptor of bruised, pitted bronze men, horses, hawks, and blank goggled heads, built up in plaster over an armature and then hacked back with a chisel.
fields.Captions: Elisabeth Frink
fields.Works: Goggle Heads; Horse and Rider, Dover Street; Walking Madonna, Salisbury Cathedral; Risen Christ, Liverpool Cathedral

fields.Title: Thomas Girtin
fields.Notes: The Eidometropolis, a 360-degree painted panorama of London exhibited in 1802, does not survive; he and Turner were exact contemporaries and friends.
fields.Description: English watercolourist who dropped the grey under-drawing and laid pure colour straight onto rough paper, giving the medium the weight of oil painting; he died at 27, and Turner said that had he lived, he himself would have starved.
fields.Captions: Thomas Girtin, painted by John Opie
fields.Works: The White House at Chelsea; Kirkstall Abbey; Bamburgh Castle; the lost Eidometropolis panorama of London

fields.Title: Robert Gober
fields.Notes: Everything is made by hand, including the fake newspapers and the wallpaper; he represented the United States at the 2001 Venice Biennale.
fields.Description: American sculptor who hand-makes things that look mass-produced -- sinks with no plumbing, playpens, wallpaper, wax legs with real hair and a drain set into the calf -- and builds them into unsettling domestic rooms.
fields.Captions: Installation view of work by Robert Gober, with hand-painted forest walls
fields.Works: Untitled (sinks) series; Untitled Leg; Prison Window; the Dia installation with painted forest walls

fields.Title: Andy Goldsworthy
fields.Notes: The photograph is usually the only surviving form of a work; the film Rivers and Tides (2001) made him widely known.
fields.Description: English land artist who builds ephemeral things outdoors from whatever is to hand -- icicles, leaves stitched with thorns, balanced stones, snowballs -- photographs them, and lets them melt, blow away or collapse.
fields.Captions: Andy Goldsworthy at work
fields.Works: Storm King Wall; Garden of Stones; Roof, National Gallery of Art; the Rain Shadows

fields.Title: Leon Golub
fields.Notes: He was married to Nancy Spero for fifty years; both were founding members of Artists and Writers Protest Against the War in Vietnam.
fields.Description: American painter of enormous unstretched canvases about power and torture -- mercenaries, interrogators, death squads -- scraped down with a meat cleaver until the raw linen shows through.
fields.Captions: Leon Golub
fields.Works: Mercenaries series; Interrogation II; Gigantomachy; Napalm

fields.Title: Jan van Goyen
fields.Notes: Some twelve hundred paintings and a thousand drawings survive; he speculated in tulips and in land, and died bankrupt.
fields.Description: Enormously prolific Dutch landscapist who narrowed his palette to browns and greys and gave two-thirds of the picture to sky -- dunes, river mouths, ferries, and ruined towers under weather.
fields.Captions: Jan van Goyen, painted by Gerard ter Borch
fields.Works: View of Dordrecht from the Dordtse Kil; River Landscape with Fishermen; Windmill by a River; Haarlemmermeer

fields.Title: Francesco Guardi
fields.Notes: The Venetian Academy admitted him only in 1784, at 72, and then only as a perspective painter.
fields.Description: Last of the great Venetian view-painters, who replaced his brother-in-law Canaletto's ruled precision with flickering, broken touches of light on water, and invented half his lagoon scenes outright.
fields.Captions: Francesco Guardi, painted by Pietro Longhi
fields.Works: The Grand Canal above the Rialto; Venice: Piazza San Marco; the capricci; the Feast Days of Doge Alvise IV Mocenigo series

fields.Title: Hans Haacke
fields.Notes: The Guggenheim cancelled his 1971 show six weeks before it opened over the Shapolsky piece and sacked the curator; Germania won the Golden Lion in 1993.
fields.Description: German-born New York artist and the sharpest practitioner of institutional critique, whose works publish the ownership of slum property, the company directorships of museum trustees, and the sources of museum money.
fields.Captions: Hans Haacke, Blue Sail
fields.Works: Shapolsky et al. Manhattan Real Estate Holdings; MoMA Poll; Germania; Condensation Cube

fields.Title: Maggi Hambling
fields.Notes: The Aldeburgh Scallop, cut with a line from Britten's Peter Grimes, has been repeatedly vandalized; the 2020 Wollstonecraft figure drew heavy criticism for being a small naked woman.
fields.Description: English painter and sculptor, the National Gallery's first artist in residence, known for portraits of a dying comedian, roaring North Sea wave paintings, and two much-attacked public sculptures in London.
fields.Captions: Maggi Hambling | A Conversation with Oscar Wilde, London, 1998
fields.Works: A Conversation with Oscar Wilde; Scallop, Aldeburgh; A Sculpture for Mary Wollstonecraft; the Max Wall and Wave series

fields.Title: Mona Hatoum
fields.Notes: Corps étranger projects an endoscopic journey through her own body onto the floor of a cylinder; Present Tense maps the Oslo Accords in red glass beads pressed into Nablus soap.
fields.Description: British-Palestinian artist, born in Beirut and stranded in London by the Lebanese civil war, who turns domestic objects into instruments of threat -- an electrified cot, a cheese grater the size of a screen, a world map in glass marbles.
fields.Captions: Mona Hatoum
fields.Works: Light Sentence; Corps étranger; Homebound; Grater Divide; Present Tense

fields.Title: Raoul Hausmann
fields.Notes: He called himself the Dadasoph; his poster-poem fmsbw is said to have set Kurt Schwitters off on the Ursonate.
fields.Description: Austrian founder-member of Berlin Dada who claimed to have invented photomontage, wrote sound poems out of randomly set type, and made an assemblage head from a wig-maker's dummy fitted with a ruler and a purse.
fields.Captions: Raoul Hausmann
fields.Works: The Spirit of Our Time (Mechanical Head); ABCD; Tatlin at Home; the optophonetic poems

fields.Title: Jan Davidsz. de Heem
fields.Notes: He moved to Antwerp in 1636, he said, because the fruit there was better to paint from; his son Cornelis carried on the manner.
fields.Description: The leading still-life painter of both the Dutch and the Flemish Baroque, who worked in Utrecht and Antwerp and piled up lavish pronk tables of lobsters, peeled lemons, glass, and silver, often with a religious edge.
fields.Captions: A Painter Smoking a Pipe, thought to be Jan Davidsz. de Heem (follower of Adriaen Brouwer) | Still Life with Books, 1628
fields.Works: Still Life with Books; A Table of Desserts; Garland of Fruit and Flowers; Eucharist in a Fruit Wreath

fields.Title: Patrick Heron
fields.Notes: He designed the big coloured-glass window at Tate St Ives; as a critic he argued that British painters had reached abstraction before the Americans did.
fields.Description: English painter and critic of the St Ives group, who moved from figurative interiors to large canvases of soft-edged, clashing colour shapes, and wrote the sharpest British art criticism of his generation.
fields.Captions: Patrick Heron, Red Garden Painting, 1985
fields.Works: Azalea Garden: May 1956; Horizontal Stripe Painting; the Tate St Ives window; Cadmium with Violet, Scarlet, Emerald, Lemon and Venetian

fields.Title: Susan Hiller
fields.Notes: She called the approach “paraconceptual”; Witness hangs several hundred small speakers in the dark, each whispering one account of a sighting.
fields.Description: American-born, London-based conceptual artist, trained as an anthropologist, who made installations out of the culture's rejected material -- automatic writing, dreams, seaside postcards, recordings of people who say they have seen UFOs.
fields.Captions: Susan Hiller
fields.Works: Witness; Dedicated to the Unknown Artists; Belshazzar's Feast; From the Freud Museum; The Last Silent Movie

fields.Title: Nicholas Hilliard
fields.Notes: He wrote The Arte of Limning, arguing against shadow in miniature painting, and was in debt for most of a career spent working for the crown.
fields.Description: Goldsmith and limner to Elizabeth I and James I, whose tiny oval portrait miniatures in bright, shadowless colour on vellum are the defining image of the Elizabethan court.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait, 1577
fields.Works: Young Man Among Roses; the Pelican and Phoenix portraits of Elizabeth I; Portrait of an Unknown Lady

fields.Title: Roger Hilton
fields.Notes: He won the John Moores prize in 1963; bedridden and alcoholic at the end, he made hundreds of small gouaches of animals and figures without getting up.
fields.Description: English painter of the St Ives circle who came back from European abstraction -- Mondrian, tachisme, CoBrA -- to a scrawled, half-figurative shorthand of nudes and beach shapes in a few blunt colours.
fields.Captions: Roger Hilton, Oi Yoi Yoi, 1963
fields.Works: Oi Yoi Yoi; February 1954; Grey Figure; the late gouaches made in bed

fields.Title: Ivon Hitchens
fields.Notes: Bombed out of his London studio in 1940, he moved to six acres of woodland at Lavington Common in Sussex and painted the same clearing for nearly forty years.
fields.Description: English painter of long, narrow, horizontal canvases in which a wood, a pond or a bridge is reduced to a few wide sweeps of loaded colour -- the place evoked rather than described.
fields.Works: Damp Autumn; the Coronation Mural at Cecil Sharp House; Winter Stage; Arno Bridge

fields.Title: Meindert Hobbema
fields.Notes: He took a job as a wine-gauger for the Amsterdam customs in 1668 and largely stopped painting; the Avenue of 1689 is a late exception.
fields.Description: Dutch Golden Age landscapist, Ruisdael's pupil, who painted wooded lanes, watermills, and dappled clearings, and once a dead-straight avenue of spindly trees running to the horizon.
fields.Captions: Drawn portrait of Meindert Hobbema | The Avenue at Middelharnis, 1689
fields.Works: The Avenue at Middelharnis; The Watermill; A Woody Landscape; The Ruins of Brederode Castle

fields.Title: Howard Hodgkin
fields.Notes: Turner Prize 1985; he worked on wood, often for years on a single picture, and always carried the paint out over the frame.
fields.Description: English painter of small, thickly worked wooden panels whose broad sweeps and blobs of hot colour, spilling over onto the frame, carry titles like Dinner at Smith Square -- memories of rooms and meetings, not abstractions.
fields.Captions: Howard Hodgkin
fields.Works: Dinner at Smith Square; Rain; In the Bay of Naples; Mr and Mrs E. J. P.

fields.Title: Ferdinand Hodler
fields.Notes: Rejected from the 1891 Geneva salon, Night made his name when it was shown in Paris; he drew and painted his dying lover almost daily through 1914 and 1915.
fields.Description: Swiss painter who called his method “parallelism”: symmetrical, frieze-like rows of near-identical figures against flat mountain or meadow grounds, alongside harsh Alpine landscapes and a series recording his lover's death.
fields.Captions: Self-Portrait with Wide-Open Eyes III, 1912
fields.Works: Night; The Chosen One; Lake Thun; the Valentine Godé-Darel death series

fields.Title: Hans Hofmann
fields.Notes: His pupils included Lee Krasner, Helen Frankenthaler, and Louise Nevelson; he closed the school in 1958, at 78, to paint full time.
fields.Description: German-born painter and, above all, teacher in Munich and New York, who brought Cubist structure and Fauve colour to a generation of Americans and preached “push and pull” -- flat colour rectangles making depth without perspective.
fields.Captions: Hans Hofmann, Effervescence, 1944
fields.Works: The Gate; Effervescence; Memoria in Aeternum; Cathedral

fields.Title: Rebecca Horn
fields.Notes: Lung damage from working with unventilated fibreglass put her in a sanatorium at 20, and the body-extension pieces began there; she also directed three feature films.
fields.Description: German artist who began with body extensions worn in performance -- finger gloves, a head-mounted horn, a feathered fan that closes round the wearer -- and went on to melancholy kinetic machines that tap, write, and bleed.
fields.Works: Unicorn (Einhorn); Pencil Mask; Concert for Anarchy; High Moon; The Tower of the Nameless

fields.Title: Peter Howson
fields.Notes: The Imperial War Museum declined Croatian and Muslim, a rape scene he had not witnessed; David Bowie bought it.
fields.Description: Scottish painter of thick-necked, over-muscled men in bleak urban and battlefield settings, one of the New Glasgow Boys, and Britain's official war artist in Bosnia in 1993.
fields.Captions: Peter Howson
fields.Works: Croatian and Muslim; Plum Grove; Patriots; The Third Step

fields.Title: Jörg Immendorff
fields.Notes: A Maoist agitator in the 1960s, he painted “Stop painting” on a canvas before returning to it; he taught at the Düsseldorf Academy and designed opera sets.
fields.Description: German Neo-Expressionist and Beuys pupil whose crowded allegorical paintings set East and West German politics inside a single nightclub full of symbols, eagles, ice, and the Brandenburg Gate.
fields.Captions: Jörg Immendorff, from the Café Deutschland series
fields.Works: Café Deutschland series; Naht; Ich wollte Künstler werden; the Beuys portraits

fields.Title: Gwen John
fields.Notes: Her brother Augustus predicted that in fifty years he would be known as her brother; she converted to Catholicism and painted the nuns of Meudon for years.
fields.Description: Welsh painter who worked in France for nearly all her career, on small, grey-toned, close-valued interiors and seated women, one sitter at a time; Rodin's model and lover, and the sister of a far more famous painter.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait, c. 1902
fields.Works: A Corner of the Artist's Room in Paris; Girl with Bare Shoulders; The Convalescent; Self-Portrait (Tate)

fields.Title: Mary Kelly
fields.Notes: The nappy-liner section, shown at the ICA in 1976, caused a tabloid outcry; the whole work runs to six parts made over six years.
fields.Description: American conceptual artist and feminist whose best-known work documents the first years of her son's life through stained nappy liners, his first words, and her own notes, laid out in the form of a scientific record.
fields.Works: Post-Partum Document; Interim; Gloria Patri; Mea Culpa

fields.Title: Ken Kiff
fields.Notes: He was in Jungian analysis for years and made The Sequence out of it; he was associate artist at the National Gallery in the 1990s.
fields.Description: English painter of dreamlike, psychologically charged scenes in acid colour -- small figures, animals, trees, and floating heads -- made under the influence of Jungian analysis and assembled into one open-ended cycle.
fields.Works: The Sequence, a cycle of some two hundred paintings; Man Greeting Woman; Talking with a Psychoanalyst; Flowers and Yellow Sky

fields.Title: R. B. Kitaj
fields.Notes: He coined “School of London” for a 1976 exhibition; a savaging of his 1994 Tate retrospective, which he blamed for his wife's death days later, drove him back to Los Angeles.
fields.Description: American painter who spent most of his life in London and named the School of London; his crowded, literary, collage-like pictures draw on Aby Warburg, Walter Benjamin, and Jewish history.
fields.Captions: R. B. Kitaj
fields.Works: The Autumn of Central Paris (after Walter Benjamin); If Not, Not; The Wedding; Cecil Court, London W.C.2

fields.Title: Laura Knight
fields.Notes: Elected RA in 1936, the first woman since the foundation members; she sat in the Nuremberg courtroom for months to paint the trial.
fields.Description: English painter in the realist tradition -- circus, ballet, gypsy encampments, Cornish cliffs, and wartime factories -- the first woman elected a full Royal Academician in the modern era, and the official artist at the Nuremberg trials.
fields.Captions: Laura Knight
fields.Works: Self-Portrait with Nude; Ruby Loftus Screwing a Breech-ring; The Nuremberg Trial; Take Off

fields.Title: Leon Kossoff
fields.Notes: He studied under David Bomberg at Borough Polytechnic alongside Frank Auerbach, and drew constantly from the Old Masters in the National Gallery.
fields.Description: English painter of the School of London whose thickly trowelled, near-sculptural paint records the same few London subjects for decades: building sites, swimming baths, Kilburn Underground, and his own family.
fields.Works: Children's Swimming Pool, Autumn Afternoon; Willesden Junction; Christ Church, Spitalfields; Portrait of Father

fields.Title: Peter Lanyon
fields.Notes: He was the only major St Ives painter born in the town; the gliding paintings of 1959 to 1964 are the culmination of the work.
fields.Description: Cornish painter of the St Ives school whose abstractions are landscapes seen from the air: he took up gliding in 1959 to paint the coast from inside the weather, and died of injuries from a gliding crash.
fields.Works: Thermal; Porthleven; St Just; Lost Mine

fields.Title: Thomas Lawrence
fields.Notes: The Waterloo Chamber at Windsor holds the series of sovereigns and commanders he painted across Europe for George IV; he died in debt despite enormous fees.
fields.Description: Child prodigy who became fourth president of the Royal Academy and the most glamorous portraitist in Europe: shimmering silks, flushed skin, and theatrical poses, painted for the Regency court and for the allied sovereigns after Waterloo.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait | Portrait of Elizabeth Farren, 1790
fields.Works: Portrait of Elizabeth Farren; Pope Pius VII; Queen Charlotte; Sarah Barrett Moulton (Pinkie)

fields.Title: Peter Lely
fields.Notes: He painted Cromwell and then Charles II; the much-repeated story that Cromwell told him to include “roughnesses, pimples, warts and everything” is the source of “warts and all”.
fields.Description: Dutch-born painter who became the dominant court portraitist of Restoration England, turning out sleepy-eyed beauties in loose satin from a large studio with assistants painting the drapery.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait | From the Windsor Beauties series, 1660s
fields.Works: Windsor Beauties series; the Flagmen of Lowestoft; Oliver Cromwell; Two Ladies of the Lake Family

fields.Title: Filippino Lippi
fields.Notes: His father Fra Filippo Lippi ran off with a nun, who was his mother; he was among the first to paint grotesques copied from the newly rediscovered Domus Aurea.
fields.Description: Florentine painter, son and pupil of a friar-painter and then of Botticelli, who finished Masaccio's Brancacci Chapel frescoes and turned late in life to a nervous, agitated style crowded with antique ornament.
fields.Captions: Presumed self-portrait, Brancacci Chapel, Florence
fields.Works: The Vision of Saint Bernard; the completion of the Brancacci Chapel; the Strozzi Chapel frescoes in Santa Maria Novella; the Carafa Chapel in Rome

fields.Title: Richard Long
fields.Notes: A Line Made by Walking (1967), made while he was a student at St Martin's, exists only as a photograph; Turner Prize 1989.
fields.Description: English land artist whose work is a walk: a line worn into a field by walking it back and forth, a circle of slate laid on a gallery floor, a text recording the miles and days of a journey.
fields.Captions: Richard Long
fields.Works: A Line Made by Walking; A Hundred Mile Walk; Stone Circle; River Avon Mud Hand Circles

fields.Title: John Martin
fields.Notes: His brother Jonathan set fire to York Minster in 1829; he spent years promoting serious engineering plans for London's sewers and water supply.
fields.Description: English Romantic painter of apocalypse on a vast scale -- cities swallowed, seas parted, armies swept away -- with pin-sized figures under colossal architecture and lightning; hugely popular in mezzotint, and detested by Ruskin.
fields.Captions: John Martin, painted by Henry Warren | The Great Day of His Wrath, 1851–53
fields.Works: The Great Day of His Wrath; Belshazzar's Feast; The Destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum; the Paradise Lost mezzotints

fields.Title: Lisa Milroy
fields.Notes: She won the John Moores prize in 1989; later work moved into painted kimonos, performance, and installation.
fields.Description: Anglo-Canadian painter known for still lifes that repeat an ordinary object -- shoes, plates, light bulbs, stamps, door handles -- in rows across a plain off-white ground, with no table and no shadow.
fields.Works: Shoes; Handles; Japanese Vases; Kimono

fields.Title: Avis Newman
fields.Notes: She has argued throughout for drawing as a primary medium in its own right rather than preparation for something else.
fields.Description: English artist who made drawing itself the primary medium: large, dark, layered surfaces of marks, veils, and half-legible traces, about memory, language, and the unconscious.
fields.Works: Large-scale drawing-paintings on unstretched canvas; The Stage of Drawing: Gesture and Act (Tate Britain and The Drawing Center, 2003), an exhibition she co-selected

fields.Title: Ben Nicholson
fields.Notes: Married to Winifred Nicholson and then to Barbara Hepworth; he and Christopher Wood found Alfred Wallis in St Ives in 1928, and he co-edited Circle in 1937.
fields.Description: English abstractionist who cut and painted shallow white reliefs of pure circles and rectangles in the 1930s, and elsewhere drew Cornish harbours and Cumberland farms in fine incised line over muted colour.
fields.Captions: Ben Nicholson as a boy, painted by his mother Mabel Pryde
fields.Works: 1934 (relief); White Relief; 1943-45 (St Ives, Cornwall); Au Chat Botté

fields.Title: Jules Olitski
fields.Notes: Clement Greenberg championed him as the best painter alive; he said he wanted “nothing but some colours sprayed into the air and staying there”, and was the first living American given a solo show at the Metropolitan Museum.
fields.Description: Russian-born American Color Field painter who sprayed acrylic mist across huge canvases so that no mark and no edge survives -- pure atmospheric colour with a crusted band left at the border.
fields.Works: Instant Loveland; High a Yellow; Green Goes Around; the Bath sculptures

fields.Title: Julian Opie
fields.Notes: The Blur cover portraits hang in the National Portrait Gallery; his walking figures loop on LED panels in cities worldwide.
fields.Description: English artist who reduces a person to a few black outlines, a filled shape, and two dots for eyes, drawn from photographs and shown as paintings, LED animations, and street sculpture; he made one of the best-known album covers of the 2000s.
fields.Captions: Julian Opie, Shaida Walking, Broadwick Street, Soho, London | Blur: The Best Of cover portraits, 2000
fields.Works: Blur: The Best Of cover portraits, 2000; Shaida Walking; Imagine you are driving; the walking-figure LED animations

fields.Title: Thérèse Oulton
fields.Notes: Shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 1987, in the prize's early years; she studied at St Martin's and the Royal College of Art.
fields.Description: English painter of dense, all-over abstract surfaces built from thousands of small strokes, which read as rock strata, folded cloth or the inside of a body without ever depicting one.
fields.Works: Fool's Gold; Letters to Raphael; Abstract with Memories; Territories

fields.Title: Samuel Palmer
fields.Notes: The Shoreham years, 1826 to 1835, were spent with the self-styled Ancients; he met William Blake in 1824, and his son burned most of the early work after his death.
fields.Description: English visionary landscape painter whose few years in a Kentish village produced small, glowing sepia and gouache pictures of swollen harvest moons, heavy corn, and hills like sleeping animals, made under Blake's spell.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait, c. 1825
fields.Works: In a Shoreham Garden; The Magic Apple Tree; Early Morning; Coming from Evening Church

fields.Title: Eduardo Paolozzi
fields.Notes: The 1947 collage contains what is often called the first appearance of the word “Pop” in an artwork; the British Library figure is Blake's Newton rebuilt as a riveted machine.
fields.Description: Scottish sculptor and printmaker of Italian descent, whose 1947 magazine collages prefigure Pop art and whose bronze figures and mosaics are assembled from cast machine parts and casts of toys.
fields.Captions: Eduardo Paolozzi, Newton, after William Blake, British Library, London
fields.Works: I was a Rich Man's Plaything; Newton, outside the British Library; the Tottenham Court Road Underground mosaics; Cyclops

fields.Title: Victor Pasmore
fields.Notes: His switch to abstraction in 1948 was called the most revolutionary event in postwar British art; he went on to design a whole housing district at Peterlee New Town.
fields.Description: English painter who began with tonal, Whistlerian Thames scenes in the Euston Road School and then, around 1948, abandoned figuration for spirals, geometric reliefs in wood and glass, and eventually town planning.
fields.Captions: Victor Pasmore
fields.Works: The Snowstorm: Spiral Motif in Black and White; the Apollo Pavilion, Peterlee; Abstract in White, Black, Brown and Lilac; The Quiet River: The Thames at Chiswick

fields.Title: A. R. Penck
fields.Notes: Born Ralf Winkler, he took the name of a geologist of the ice ages to smuggle work westward; he also drummed in free-jazz groups.
fields.Description: East German Neo-Expressionist who painted stick figures, arrows, and signs in a deliberately primitive code -- part cave painting, part circuit diagram -- as a way of writing about a divided country; he worked under a false name and was expelled to the West in 1980.
fields.Captions: A. R. Penck, photographed by Oliver Mark
fields.Works: Weltbild (World Picture) paintings; the Standart series; Übergang (Crossing); N. Komplex

fields.Title: Piero di Cosimo
fields.Notes: Vasari says he lived on hard-boiled eggs, boiled fifty at a time while boiling his glue, and would not let his room be swept or his fruit trees pruned.
fields.Description: Eccentric Florentine painter who kept an Early Renaissance manner into the 16th century and specialized in strange mythological scenes -- centaurs, satyrs, hunts, forest fires, prehistoric humanity -- full of closely observed animals.
fields.Captions: Piero di Cosimo, Perseus Freeing Andromeda, c. 1510–15 | The Forest Fire, c. 1505
fields.Works: The Forest Fire; A Satyr Mourning over a Nymph; Perseus Freeing Andromeda; The Hunt

fields.Title: John Piper
fields.Notes: An official war artist recording bomb damage, he was also Benjamin Britten's designer; the Coventry window runs to 195 separate lights.
fields.Description: English painter and designer who abandoned abstraction for dark, romantic views of bombed churches and country houses, and made stained glass for Coventry Cathedral as well as opera sets for Britten.
fields.Captions: John Piper
fields.Works: Coventry Cathedral baptistry window; All Saints Chapel, Bath; Seaton Delaval; the Recording Britain watercolours

fields.Title: Sigmar Polke
fields.Notes: Golden Lion at the 1986 Venice Biennale for a pavilion whose paint changed colour with the humidity; he replaced the medieval windows of Zurich's Grossmünster with sliced agate.
fields.Description: German painter who founded Capitalist Realism with Gerhard Richter as a jab at both Pop art and Socialist Realism, blew up newspaper half-tone dots by hand, and later let toxic chemicals and minerals react on the canvas.
fields.Captions: Sigmar Polke
fields.Works: Bunnies; the Watchtower series; Girlfriends; the Grossmünster windows in Zurich

fields.Title: Antonio del Pollaiolo
fields.Notes: He worked with his brother Piero; Vasari credits him with dissecting bodies to study the muscles, and the two papal tombs in St Peter's are his.
fields.Description: Florentine goldsmith, painter, sculptor, and engraver who studied the body in violent motion, and made the first important Italian engraving: ten naked men fighting in a thicket for no stated reason.
fields.Captions: Portrait bust of Antonio del Pollaiolo from the brothers' tomb, San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome | Battle of the Nude Men, c. 1470
fields.Works: Battle of the Nude Men; Hercules and Antaeus; Martyrdom of Saint Sebastian; the tombs of Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII

fields.Title: Paula Rego
fields.Notes: The 1998 Abortion pastels are widely credited with helping shift the second Portuguese referendum in 2007; she was the National Gallery's first associate artist.
fields.Description: Portuguese-British painter of thickset women in unsettling storybook scenes -- nursery rhymes, folk tales, Jane Eyre -- worked in pastel at near life size, including a series made against Portugal's abortion ban.
fields.Captions: Paula Rego
fields.Works: The Family; the Dog Woman series; the Abortion pastels; The Dance; the Snow White series

fields.Title: Germaine Richier
fields.Notes: She trained under Bourdelle, Rodin's assistant; her 1950 crucifix for Assy was removed after Vatican objections and only reinstated in 1969.
fields.Description: French sculptor of corroded, half-devoured bronze figures fused with insects, plants, and bats -- a praying-mantis woman, a storm-battered man -- expressing postwar anxiety about the body.
fields.Captions: Germaine Richier in her studio
fields.Works: The Praying Mantis (La Mante); L'Orage (The Storm); The Bat; the crucifix for the church at Assy

fields.Title: George Romney
fields.Notes: Emma Hart became Lady Hamilton and Nelson's mistress; he left his wife in Kendal for nearly forty years and returned to her only to die.
fields.Description: English portraitist, the third of the great Georgian trio with Reynolds and Gainsborough, who never exhibited at the Royal Academy and painted his obsession, Emma Hart, some sixty times in mythological guises.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait, 1795
fields.Works: Emma Hart as Circe; Lady Hamilton as a Bacchante; The Leveson-Gower Children; Mrs Carwardine and Son

fields.Title: Salvator Rosa
fields.Notes: That self-portrait is inscribed “Keep silent unless what you have to say is better than silence”; his satires made him so many enemies that he kept moving between Naples, Rome, and Florence.
fields.Description: Neapolitan Baroque painter, poet, satirist, and actor whose wild, stormy landscapes with banditti, blasted trees, and hermits became the 18th century's model for the Sublime and a hero to the Romantics.
fields.Captions: Self-portrait, c. 1650–60
fields.Works: Landscape with Bandits; Witches at their Incantations; Saul and the Witch of Endor; the National Gallery self-portrait

fields.Title: James Rosenquist
fields.Notes: F-111 is 26 metres long and was made to wrap round all four walls of a gallery, setting a fighter-bomber against consumer imagery at the height of Vietnam.
fields.Description: American Pop artist who learned his trade painting billboards above Times Square and applied it to enormous fragmented canvases where spaghetti, a Ford grille, a bomber, and a hair dryer are spliced together.
fields.Captions: James Rosenquist
fields.Works: F-111; President Elect; I Love You with My Ford; Star Thief

fields.Title: Susan Rothenberg
fields.Notes: The horse, she said, was a way of making a figure that was not a figure; she later moved to New Mexico with her husband Bruce Nauman.
fields.Description: American painter who broke out of Minimalism in the 1970s with flat, ghostly horse silhouettes crossed by a dividing line, and later made twisting, all-over pictures of bodies, dogs, and hands in heavy brushwork.
fields.Captions: Susan Rothenberg
fields.Works: Butterfly; Axes; IXI; Blue Head

fields.Title: Georges Rouault
fields.Notes: Apprenticed to a glass painter at 14 and then Gustave Moreau's favourite pupil; he burned 315 of his own unfinished paintings in 1948 after winning a lawsuit against his dealer's heirs.
fields.Description: French painter trained as a stained-glass restorer, whose clowns, prostitutes, judges, and Christs are laid on in thick, glowing colour inside heavy black outlines like lead cames; a Fauve by association and a Catholic moralist by conviction.
fields.Captions: Georges Rouault (right) in his later years
fields.Works: Miserere print series; The Old King; Head of Christ; The Three Judges

fields.Title: Sean Scully
fields.Notes: Twice shortlisted for the Turner Prize; the Wall of Light series began from watercolours of Mayan stonework in Mexico.
fields.Description: Irish-born American painter of stacked and interlocking bands of colour, built in thick oil with brushed, uneven edges, so that the geometry stays hand-made and emotional rather than Minimalist.
fields.Captions: Sean Scully
fields.Works: Wall of Light series; Backs and Fronts; Paul; the Landline series

fields.Title: Walter Sickert
fields.Notes: Founder of the Camden Town Group; a persistent amateur theory, revived by Patricia Cornwell, names him as Jack the Ripper on no serious evidence.
fields.Description: German-born British painter, Whistler's assistant, and Degas's follower, who painted music halls, shabby Camden bedrooms, and a notorious series showing a clothed man and a naked woman in a squalid interior.
fields.Captions: Walter Sickert
fields.Works: Ennui; the Camden Town Murder series; La Hollandaise; Minnie Cunningham at the Old Bedford

fields.Title: Pierre Soulages
fields.Notes: He designed 104 windows for the Romanesque abbey at Conques in a translucent white glass he developed himself; a museum of his work opened in Rodez in 2014.
fields.Description: French painter who spent sixty years on black, and from 1979 on black alone -- outrenoir -- scraping ridges and furrows into thick paint so that the surface throws light back in bands.
fields.Captions: Pierre Soulages
fields.Works: Outrenoir paintings, from 1979; Peinture, 1956; the windows of the abbey church at Conques

fields.Title: Stanley Spencer
fields.Notes: He called Cookham “a village in Heaven”; the Sandham murals come out of his service as a medical orderly and in Macedonia in the First World War.
fields.Description: English painter who set the Resurrection, the Crucifixion, and the Last Supper in the Berkshire village where he was born, with neighbours climbing out of the churchyard graves in their Sunday clothes.
fields.Captions: William McBrearty, Sawyer, from Shipbuilding on the Clyde, 1943–44
fields.Works: The Resurrection, Cookham; the Sandham Memorial Chapel murals; Shipbuilding on the Clyde; Christ Carrying the Cross

fields.Title: Nancy Spero
fields.Notes: Married to Leon Golub; she was a founder of A.I.R., New York's first women's cooperative gallery, in 1972.
fields.Description: American artist who worked only on paper, in scrolls metres long, printing and stamping small figures of women taken from myth, Greek vases, and news photographs, alongside texts about war and torture.
fields.Captions: Nancy Spero in her studio
fields.Works: Torture of Women; The War Series; Notes in Time on Women; Codex Artaud

fields.Title: Nicolas de Staël
fields.Notes: The football paintings came from watching a floodlit France-Sweden match in 1952; he jumped from his studio terrace in Antibes three years later.
fields.Description: Russian-born French painter who laid thick, mosaic-like slabs of colour on with a knife, moving between abstraction and just-legible footballers, bottles and Mediterranean skies before killing himself at 41.
fields.Captions: Nicolas de Staël
fields.Works: Les Footballeurs (Parc des Princes); Agrigente; Le Lavandou; Composition

fields.Title: Philip Wilson Steer
fields.Notes: A founder of the New English Art Club, set up against the Royal Academy; his Slade pupils included Augustus John, Gwen John, and Stanley Spencer.
fields.Description: English painter who brought French Impressionism home in beach and seaside scenes of the 1880s and 90s, then retreated into a Constable-and-Turner English landscape manner; he taught at the Slade for nearly forty years.
fields.Captions: Philip Wilson Steer
fields.Works: Boulogne Sands; Girls Running, Walberswick Pier; The Bridge; Chepstow Castle

fields.Title: Graham Sutherland
